comments.author: Claude
comments.text: retro: check-skills.sh rejects a bare backticked script name — it resolves `bb-checks.py` relative to the citing file and errors when it does not exist there. The convention that passes is the `scripts/` prefix (the checker skips anything starting with it), which is why `scripts/bb-status.sh` is written that way throughout. Four files hit it; the gate caught all four before the commit.

comments.author: Claude
comments.text: retro: project-setup.md's command-permissions list named the checks script's own path as an entry to allow. Under a declaration there is no such path — the runner is one bundled-script entry like the others, and what needs allowing is whatever the declared commands invoke underneath. Restructured rather than renamed.

comments.author: Claude
comments.text: retro: bead-bonanza/SKILL.md went 57374 -> 57321 body bytes across this epic, so the known-red size warning moved down rather than up. Worth recording because the acceptance only asked that it not grow, and a rewrite of nine call sites could easily have added a few hundred bytes without anyone noticing.

comments.author: Claude
comments.text: retro: the load-bearing sentence in run-bead step 4 turned out to be 'a narrowed run is a fast loop, never the gate'. Without it, giving an agent ids to target reads as permission to close on a subset — which is the slim-gates failure mode arriving by a different door.

title: bb-checks.sh — parse, validate and run declared checks
description:
Ship plugin/skills/bead-bonanza/scripts/bb-checks.sh. It is the runner the plugin owns so no project has to write one.

Plan: docs/plans/sf-toml-declared-checks.md sections 2 and 3 (S1). The contract is pinned there; implement it, do not redesign it.

Behaviour:
- Resolve repo root with `git rev-parse --show-toplevel`.
- Parse sf.toml with python3 tomllib (stdlib since 3.11; this container is 3.11.15). Do NOT hand-roll [[checks]] in awk — sf_get's reader cannot do array-of-tables and restricted parsing of a real format is the fragility class this review has been removing. Assert python3 at the top with a message naming what is missing, the way jq is already asserted in pre-flight.
- Validate the WHOLE array before running anything: id matches [a-z0-9][a-z0-9-]*, unique; command a non-empty string; no other keys accepted. An unrecognised key is a hard error, never ignored — a typo that silently dropped a check would read downstream as a check that passed.
- Execute via `sh -c`, cwd = repository root, environment inherited.
- Serial, in DECLARATION order, always — including when ids are passed as arguments, so `bb-checks.sh build schemas` runs them in declared order rather than argument order. Never reorder, never parallelise.
- Run every requested check even after one fails.

Interface: no args runs all; `<id>...` runs those; `--ids` prints declared ids one per line; `--self-test`.

Output: `=== <id>` before and `=== <id> FAILED (exit N)` after a failing check, both on stderr, with the command's own streams passed through untouched between them.

Exit: 0 all requested passed, 1 at least one failed, 3 invocation or configuration error (malformed TOML, no [[checks]], duplicate id, unknown key, missing command, unknown id argument). A 3 runs NOTHING — a bad declaration must not half-execute. These match bb-status.sh's convention.

sf_get stays where it is: [models] and [run] are flat key reads and need no parser.

Nothing consumes this yet; it lands standalone.
acceptance_criteria: bb-checks.py --self-test exits 0 and covers every row of the plan's section 4 matrix: two passing checks; first fails and second still runs; duplicate id; unknown key; missing command; malformed id; malformed TOML; no [[checks]] array (message distinct from empty array); empty array; checks not an array of tables; args given out of declaration order run in declaration order; a subset runs only what was asked; unknown id argument exits 3 having run nothing; --ids in declaration order; --ids on an invalid declaration exits 3; a check that cd's does not move the next one. Fixtures are generated into a temp git repo by the self-test itself.

comments.author: Claude
comments.text: retro: the acceptance said fixtures live beside the script; they are generated into a temp git repo by --self-test instead. Committed fixtures would ship to every project that vendors this plugin as dead weight, and the fixture body is more useful sitting next to the assertion that reads it. Acceptance updated rather than quietly diverged from.

comments.author: Claude
comments.text: retro: wrote the whole runner in python3 rather than the plan's shell-plus-python hybrid, and renamed it bb-checks.py. The plan pinned python3 tomllib for parsing (decision 9), which makes python3 a hard dependency either way; splitting parse from execute would then have needed a serialization boundary between them, and TOML literal strings can legally contain newlines, so any delimiter choice could be defeated by a valid command. Running via subprocess with inherited fds also passes tool output through byte for byte, where a shell loop re-emitting captured text could not.

comments.author: Claude
comments.text: retro: added three validation cases the plan's matrix did not name — an id failing the slug pattern, a non-empty checks key that is not an array of tables, and --ids on an invalid declaration. Each is reachable by an ordinary typo, and all three must exit 3 having run nothing for the 'a bad declaration must not half-execute' rule to mean anything.

comments.author: Claude
comments.text: retro: the cwd assertion failed on first run and the defect was the fixture, not the runner — it tested for sf.toml in a temp repo that has none. Worth noting because a self-test that had asserted something weaker would have passed and proven nothing; the fix was to plant a marker file reachable only from the root.

title: Pre-flight resolves and baselines through bb-checks.sh
description:
Plan: docs/plans/sf-toml-declared-checks.md S2.

In plugin/skills/bead-bonanza/scripts/pre-flight-check.sh:

Section 2 — replace the `sf_get checkpoints checks` resolution block. Locate bb-checks.sh, run `--ids`, and block the run when the declaration is absent or invalid, QUOTING the runner's own error rather than restating it. Emit BB_CHECKS_IDS (space-separated). BB_CHECKS (a path) goes away.

Resolution collapses to ONE mechanism: [[checks]] in sf.toml, with $BB_SF_TOML overriding the file's location (fixtures and self-test need it). The [checkpoints] checks key, $BB_CHECKS and the scripts/checks fallback are REMOVED, not kept alongside — two ways to declare the same thing is a fork in the contract, and nothing outside this branch has used either. A project wanting one script declares one entry pointing at it.

Section 8 — baseline capture runs bb-checks.sh and writes $RUN_DIR/checks-baseline.md as it does today. The captured text now carries === <id> delimiters, so add a per-check verdict summary above the raw block, derived from them. Keep the existing distinction between a baseline that exited 0 and one that was already failing, and keep 'not captured' as a third, differently-worded state.
acceptance_criteria: Pre-flight blocks with the runner's own message when sf.toml declares no valid [[checks]]; emits BB_CHECKS_IDS and no BB_CHECKS; writes a baseline carrying both the per-check summary and the raw delimited output; $BB_SF_TOML redirects the config file. scripts/checks (still present at this point) is no longer consulted.

comments.author: Claude
comments.text: retro: verified end to end rather than by reading. Ran pre-flight with BB_SF_TOML pointed at a three-check fixture (green / red-exiting-4 / also-green) and confirmed the generated checks-baseline.md carries the per-check verdict table AND the raw delimited block, and that also-green ran after red failed — the run-every-check rule proven through the whole path, not just in the runner's own self-test. Pre-flight exited 1 on two unrelated environmental blockers (dirty tree mid-bead, unset worktree.baseRef).

comments.author: Claude
comments.text: retro: moved sf_get's definition down to sit with its callers and made it read \${BB_SF_TOML:-sf.toml}. It had been hardcoded to sf.toml, so with BB_SF_TOML set the checks would have come from the fixture while [models] and [run] came from the real file — two halves of one config resolving to different files. Not something the bead named; found by using the override.

comments.author: Claude
comments.text: retro: added python3 3.11+ as a blocking dependency next to jq, probing 'import tomllib' rather than a version string — the import settles interpreter and version in one call. The plan named python3 as a hard dependency but no bead said where it gets asserted, and an unasserted dependency fails at the baseline instead of at pre-flight.

title: Declared checks in sf.toml
description:
Replace the single executable `checks` script with an array of declared checks in sf.toml, each carrying an `id` and a `command`. A plugin-shipped runner (bb-checks.sh) executes them; the project supplies commands, not a protocol.

Full plan, including the pinned contract and the verification matrix: docs/plans/sf-toml-declared-checks.md. Read it before starting any child — the ten decisions in section 6 are settled and are not to be re-litigated mid-implementation.

Why: the floor to adopt bead-bonanza drops from 'write an executable' to four lines of TOML; 'run every check even after one fails' stops being a convention the project must remember and becomes the runner's job; and per-check ids make targeted runs possible without asking the project for a path-to-check mapping.

What does NOT change: each command's own exit status is its verdict, nothing parses tool output, and attribution stays a bead comparing its own raw output against the baseline's. This moves where the list of commands lives, not what a check must emit.
acceptance_criteria: A project declares checks as [[checks]] entries in sf.toml; bb-checks.sh runs them serially in declaration order, runs every requested one even after a failure, and exits 0/1/3; pre-flight resolves and baselines through it; the prompt and skill surfaces name declared ids; this repository is migrated and scripts/checks is deleted; ADR-022 records the decision.

comments.author: Claude
comments.text: retro: deleted docs/plans/sf-toml-declared-checks.md on close. AGENTS.md classifies docs/plans/ as transient — delete when the change lands — and the plan said the same of itself. Its durable content is now in ADR-022 (the contract and why the ids live in config), in bb-checks.py's header (the interface), and in project-setup.md (what a project writes). Recoverable from git history if the PR review still wants it.

comments.author: Claude
comments.text: retro: the one design change the plan did not anticipate was --report. The pinned contract made the '=== <id> FAILED (exit N)' delimiter the machine-readable verdict, and that is forgeable by any tool the runner invokes — measured during migration, with a check that echoed a FAILED line for a passing sibling and successfully flipped its verdict in the baseline table. Verdicts moved out of band; the delimiters stayed as a reading aid.

comments.author: Claude
comments.text: retro: the epic's four beads were sequenced runner -> pre-flight -> (surfaces | migration), and taking the migration before the surfaces meant every bead after it gated through the new runner rather than the one being replaced. That was not planned and is worth doing deliberately next time: the tool that replaces a gate should gate its own remaining work.

title: Say what belongs in the checks script, and why batching exists
description:
Two corrections from PR #27 review.

1. The checks script's SCOPE is undocumented. It is the subset a project wants run after every bead — deliberately not the full CI suite, so that running it per bead is affordable. project-setup.md currently tells an author to discover candidates from 'build/test/lint/format sections, CI config', which invites putting a multi-minute harness in it. Measured elsewhere by the reviewer: some test harnesses take ~6 minutes, which would cripple a run if invoked per bead. Without this premise stated, 'run the checks before every close' reads as unaffordable.

This is not a return of slim gates. The selection is the PROJECT's, made once when it writes the script; bead-bonanza still runs whatever it finds, in full, every time.

2. Batching's rationale is misstated. It is not dispatch cost and it is not surface context: beads are batched so that beads which cannot safely run in parallel are grouped behind one agent, letting the rest of the wave dispatch in parallel around them. Stated wrong in plan-sprint/SKILL.md (two places) and subagent-prompts.md (one).
acceptance_criteria: project-setup.md states the checks script is the per-bead set and that slow whole-repo checks belong in CI; ADR-022 carries the same in one sentence; the declared-checks plan says the array is the per-bead set; no document claims batching saves dispatches or exists for surface context; check-skills.sh --strict shows no findings beyond baseline.

comments.author: Claude
comments.text: retro: the checks script's affordability premise was never written down anywhere — not in project-setup.md, not in ADR-022, not in the ceremony. Every document described HOW to declare and run it; none said what belongs in it. That absence is what let 'run it per bead' read as expensive and made 'skip it between beads' look like the reasonable trade.

comments.author: Claude
comments.text: retro: ran spec check --strict (built from cli/spec, not cli/cmd/spec — the workflow's path is ./spec) because this touched an ADR; it is not one of scripts/checks' nine gates and exists only in CI's corpus job. A bead editing specs/ has no local gate covering it unless it thinks to build the CLI.

comments.author: Claude
comments.text: retro: I restated batching's rationale twice in two hours and got it wrong both times — first dispatch cost, then shared-surface context. The actual reason is that batching is what makes a wave parallelizable: beads that would collide go behind one agent so the rest can dispatch concurrently. Both wrong answers were plausible readings of the surrounding text, which is a sign the reason was never stated, only implied by the mode names.

title: Every bead runs checks before its own close, batched or not
description:
The batch templates in references/subagent-prompts.md told the subagent NOT to run the project's checks script between beads, then attributed a batch-end failure to 'the most-recent bead'. That inference is invalid: with no per-bead run, nothing establishes that the earlier beads were ever clean.

Worse, both batch templates invoke the `run-bead` skill per bead, whose step 4 requires the checks script to run before the close. The batch templates were overriding the ceremony they dispatch.

Decision (reviewer, PR #27): every bead runs the project's checks script AND its own targeted tests before committing, batched or not. Batching no longer saves check runs; it saves one dispatch instead of N, one worktree, and one agent holding a shared surface's context.

This premise is also stated in bead-bonanza/SKILL.md in three places (the tier-batching cost weighing, the over-route table example, and the 'push is the gate' / 'reduced gates' operating principles), all of which now contradict it.

plan-sprint/SKILL.md is a fourth surface: its entire batching rationale was test-suite amortization ('Batching N beads saves N-1 full test runs', 'Batching's saving is test-suite amortization', 'Saves N-1 full test-suite runs', and a >=2 threshold justified by 'one fewer full test run'). With checks per bead that argument is gone and the real saving has to be stated instead.
acceptance_criteria: No batch template instructs skipping the checks script between beads; no text attributes a batch-end finding to the most-recent bead on the strength of a run that did not happen; SKILL.md's batching rationale, over-route example and push-is-the-gate principle state the per-bead rule; 'reduced gates' vocabulary is gone; check-skills.sh --strict shows no findings beyond baseline and SKILL.md does not grow.

comments.author: Claude
comments.text: retro: the invalid inference was load-bearing further up than it looked. 'The most-recent bead is the suspect' only holds if the earlier beads were each shown clean, and nothing established that — plan-sprint had built a whole dispatch-mode rationale on the same premise, down to a >=2 batching threshold justified by 'one fewer full test run'. Fixing the two lines the review flagged without following the premise would have left three files arguing for the behaviour the fix removed.

comments.author: Claude
comments.text: retro: had to restate what batching buys, since amortization was the only rationale on record. Settled on: one dispatch instead of N, one worktree, one merge, and — for a shared surface — one agent holding that surface's context, which is the opposite of what isolating those beads does. That last point is the strongest and was previously unstated.

comments.author: Claude
comments.text: retro: the batch templates were overriding the ceremony they dispatch. Both invoke `run-bead` per bead, whose step 4 requires the checks script before the close, and then instructed the subagent to skip it. Neither document referenced the other, so nothing caught it — the contradiction was only visible by reading both at once.

title: Clear dead gate-profile placeholders from dispatch prompts
description:
`references/subagent-prompts.md` interpolates {FORMAT} {LINT} {BUILD} {TEST} {REGEN} {CUSTOM_GATES} in ten places, and `plan-sprint/references/dispatch-plan.md` carries a matching 'Gate profile' manifest row. Pre-flight stopped parsing AGENTS.md for gate commands and emits none of these facts, so every dispatched prompt currently carries placeholders that resolve to nothing.

Also dead in the same lines: 'the profile' as a source of targeted tests, custom gates and a regen command (the gate profile mechanism it named is gone), and the {CHECKS_BASELINE} placeholder, which is ambiguous between the BB_CHECKS_BASELINE status word and the file contents the surrounding instruction asks to be inlined.

The batch templates express reduced per-bead validation by naming individual gates, which the one-script checks contract cannot express. Re-express as: targeted tests between beads, the full checks script once at batch end.
acceptance_criteria: No {FORMAT}/{LINT}/{BUILD}/{TEST}/{REGEN}/{CUSTOM_GATES} placeholder remains anywhere in plugin/; no reference to 'the profile' as a source of gate commands remains; the baseline placeholder is unambiguous; the batch templates' reduced-validation strategy is expressible under the one-script contract; check-skills.sh --strict shows no findings beyond the recorded baseline.

comments.author: Claude
comments.text: retro: the residue spanned three files, not one. plan-sprint/references/dispatch-plan.md carried a matching 'Gate profile' manifest row fed directly by subagent-prompts.md's grooming template, and bead-bonanza/SKILL.md cited BB_LINT and BB_MTIME as example pre-flight facts — pre-flight emits neither. Cleaning only the named file would have left the consumer of its output stale.

comments.author: Claude
comments.text: retro: {CHECKS_BASELINE} was ambiguous rather than merely stale — pre-flight emits BB_CHECKS_BASELINE as a one-word status (captured/skipped), while the surrounding instruction asked for the file's contents inlined. An orchestrator substituting the emitted fact would have produced 'Checks baseline: captured' and no baseline at all. Renamed to {CHECKS_BASELINE_TEXT} and the distinction stated.

comments.author: Claude
comments.text: retro: the batch templates could not simply have their placeholders swapped. They expressed reduced per-bead validation by NAMING individual gates (run format+build, skip test), which the one-script contract cannot express at all. Re-expressed as: targeted tests between beads, the full checks script once at batch end — same intent, sayable under the current contract.

comments.author: Claude
comments.text: retro: the known-red check-skills.sh --strict baseline moved by 4 bytes (57370 -> 57374 on bead-bonanza/SKILL.md) because this bead edited that file. Same warning, same count, same verdict — the figure is the moving body size AGENTS.md warns not to record.

title: Reduce the checks contract to: run the script, read the exit code
description:
## Context

Follow-up to the contract reduction. The remaining requirement — emit `RESULT <gate> <verdict> <exit>` per gate — makes every project invent ids for its checks and echo a line per check.

It bought nothing. The justification was that the baseline needs per-gate verdicts to distinguish a known-red gate from a new failure, but the baseline is the tools' RAW OUTPUT and the bar is a comparison against it: a line in both was already there, a line only in yours is yours. That comparison never reads a gate name.

Start simple; add structure when something actually needs it.

## Success Criteria

- [ ] The contract is: run the script; exit 0 means everything passed; output is whatever the tools printed.
- [ ] No required output format, no gate ids, no stdout/stderr split rule.
- [ ] The checks baseline is the combined output plus the exit code.
- [ ] `BB_GATE_*` per-gate facts are removed; nothing downstream reads a gate name.
- [ ] One piece of guidance survives: run every check even after one fails, so the output shows all of them — chaining with `&&` hides everything after the first failure.
- [ ] This repository's own script keeps accepting names as a local convenience, stated as NOT part of the contract.
- [ ] ADR-022 re-amended; corpus validates.

title: One durable pipefail rule in AGENTS.md, replacing the per-instance entries
description:
## Context

Second instance this session of the same class: under `set -o pipefail`, a reader that closes the pipe early makes a successful writer report failure. First was `$?` read through a pager (already in the ledger); second was `bd show <id> | grep -qi closed` reporting a CLOSED bead as not closed, because grep -q exits at the first match and bd takes SIGPIPE.

Fixing these one at a time is the wrong shape — it is one rule.

## Success Criteria

- [ ] AGENTS.md carries a single rule covering the class: `grep -q`, `head`, `tail` and any early-closing reader.
- [ ] It names the symptom (a command that succeeded reports failure) so a reader recognises it from the outside.
- [ ] The existing per-instance ledger entry is folded into it rather than left alongside.
- [ ] It sits where a script author reads before writing, not only in the failure ledger.

title: Delete slim gates; the checks script runs after every bead
description:
## Context

Slim gates let a batch skip its full suite when a PR was open so pushes triggered CI. Two problems, both surfaced on PR #27.

The premise is false here: this repository's workflows are guarded `if: github.event.pull_request.draft == false`, so a draft PR runs nothing — measured on PR #27, where all five checks reported `skipped` across 41 commits.

More importantly the owner does not want the optimization at all: the checks script exists so the project's checks run after **every** dev task. When CI runs is the project's policy, and some teams do not use GitHub.

## Success Criteria

- [ ] `{SLIM_GATES}` and the slim-gates branch are removed from every dispatch template.
- [ ] The batch templates run the full checks script after every bead, with no skip path.
- [ ] The Phase 0 draft-PR question and `BB_PR_CI` go with it — the skill neither asks nor measures whether a PR would trigger CI.
- [ ] Nothing in the skill prescribes a PR workflow; where a project runs CI on a PR, that is stated as the project's, and the run consumes it rather than imposing it.

title: Reduce the checks contract to a bare command with no subcommand
description:
## Context

Review on PR #27: the three-subcommand contract (`list`/`run`/`targeted`) is more than the evidence supports. `run` is load-bearing — without a verdict per gate the baseline cannot tell a known-red gate from one this bead broke. `list` is a second way to learn what `run` already prints. `targeted` has no evidence it earns a required subcommand.

With one subcommand left there is no need for a subcommand at all.

## Success Criteria

- [ ] The contract is `checks [<gate>...]` — no args runs everything, in declared order.
- [ ] Output rule unchanged: `RESULT <gate> <pass|fail|skip> <exit>` on stdout, the tools' own output on stderr, exit 0/1/2.
- [ ] `list` and `targeted` are gone from the required contract; a project may still add its own subcommands.
- [ ] Pre-flight stops calling `list`; it derives gate ids from the baseline run's RESULT lines.
- [ ] `references/project-setup.md` shrinks to the contract table, with no rationale prose.
- [ ] ADR-022's Decision is re-amended to match, and the corpus still validates.

title: Deliver the gate baseline to the agent that runs the gate
description:
## Context

ADR-022's central defect is still live after the checks-script change. Pre-flight captures a baseline (`BB_GATE_*=pass|fail`) and it reaches the grooming/planning prompt — and stops there. The per-bead prompt has no baseline field, and its gate step says only "On gate failure, fix the root cause and rerun".

So on any known-red gate every bead is told to fix a failure that is not its own. This repository has such a gate (`skills-strict`), so the defect fires on its own runs.

Discovered while implementing the checks script; out of that bead's acceptance criteria, which covered the entry point rather than the delivery.

## Success Criteria

- [ ] The run's known-red state is written once to a run-scoped file, per ADR-022 — the gate baseline and the environmental-failure ledger in one place, which is what SKILL.md already claims the ledger is.
- [ ] A rendered summary is inlined into every subagent prompt, **including when it is empty**, so "nothing known-red" and "not measured" are distinguishable.
- [ ] The per-bead gate step tells the agent which failures are pre-existing and correct to leave.
- [ ] Demonstrated on this repository, whose `skills-strict` gate is known-red.

title: Spike: CLAUDE_CODE_SUBAGENT_MODEL precedence, probed with the variable set at launch
description:
## Goal

Settle whether `CLAUDE_CODE_SUBAGENT_MODEL` overrides the per-invocation `model` parameter, which is the premise E6 deletes both routing tables on.

## Context

S1 (`agent-plugins-epju`) measured the half that was reachable from inside a running session and could not measure this half. With the variable unset, the `model` parameter demonstrably routes: two subagents dispatched in one session were served by `claude-haiku-4-5-20251001` and `claude-opus-5` respectively, read from their own transcripts rather than self-report.

The variable was `NOTSET` in the session and in both subagents, and it cannot be injected into an already-running session — exporting it from a Bash tool call does not reach the process that dispatches subagents. So the precedence question needs the variable present before the CLI starts.

## Method

- [ ] Set `CLAUDE_CODE_SUBAGENT_MODEL` to a model outside the project lineup, at container or CLI launch (environment variable on the cloud environment, or `export` before `claude` locally).
- [ ] Confirm it is visible: `env | grep CLAUDE_CODE_SUBAGENT_MODEL` from inside a session.
- [ ] Dispatch two subagents differing only in the `model` parameter.
- [ ] Read each subagent's serving model from its own transcript (`"model"` on its assistant messages), not from self-report — S1 established that `get_session` reports the PARENT session's model and so cannot answer this.
- [ ] State which precedence rule holds.

## Findings

_Not yet run._ Record the command executed, the conditions it ran under, and the result observed — per AGENTS.md's ledger admission rule. State an explicit `no action` if the finding changes nothing.

title: Configure sync.remote normally; pull at session start, push at turn end
description:
## Problem

`.beads/config.yaml` deliberately omitted `sync.remote` and the SessionStart hook stripped the key every session. The rationale was a bd 1.2.1 behaviour ("looks like a git code-repository URL, not a Dolt remote — skipping clone", followed by a false "Database already exists"). bd 1.2.2 does not have it.

Costs of the workaround:
- `bd prime` told every agent "No git remote configured. Issues are saved locally only" and omitted `bd dolt push`/`pull` from its command reference — the tracker's own guidance contradicted how this repo works, every session.
- Persistence outside the close ceremony depended on an agent remembering `bd dolt push`.
- The hook never pulled on a non-empty tracker, so a reused container ran against a stale database.

## Change

- `.beads/config.yaml`: `sync.remote: "git+https://github.com/brettcallaghan/agent-plugins.git"`, the value bd derives itself. File cut 112 -> 37 lines.
- `.claude/hooks/session-start.sh`: strip block deleted; non-empty tracker now runs `bd dolt pull`.
- `.claude/hooks/dolt-push.sh` + Stop hook: `bd dolt push` at the end of every turn (~2s, no-op safe, never fails the turn, `BB_DOLT_AUTOPUSH=0` opts out).
- `.beads/metadata.json`: trailing newline removed so bootstrap leaves the tree clean.

## Success Criteria

- [x] Fresh clone + committed config bootstraps 317 issues and pulls/pushes
- [x] The `.git` suffix is accepted (it is what bd derives)
- [x] `bd bootstrap` leaves the tracked tree clean — `git status --porcelain` empty
- [x] `bd prime` emits the Dolt sync commands again

title: Spike: does a Monitor over a polled command match tail -F?
description:
## Goal

Settle, by measurement: does a Monitor over a polled command match tail -F.

## Context

Deleting the progress ledger (E1) removes the run's only push signal: `tail -F` wakes the Monitor the moment an event lands, where `git log` must be polled. The replacement is a Monitor over `git log --oneline <branch>` - one line per bead close, which is exactly the `committed` event the Monitor already filters for, taken from state instead of testimony. Unmeasured.

Plan: `docs/plans/bead-bonanza-renovation.md`. Review evidence: `docs/research/bead-bonanza-design/README.md`.

## Method

- [ ] Arm a Monitor of each kind over one wave.
- [ ] Record wake latency and whether the polled form misses events.
- [ ] State whether the polled form is an acceptable replacement, and at what interval.

## Findings

**Not run — SUPERSEDED by S5 (`agent-plugins-89gy`), per this spike's own
contingency ("may supersede S4 entirely").**

S5 established that `bd` fires an issue-level `on_update` script hook from the
tracker write itself: executable `.beads/hooks/on_update`, invoked with the
issue id and the full issue JSON on stdin, on every status change including the
close. That supplies the push signal the progress ledger uniquely provided,
without a subagent-written file and without testimony — the hook can append the
line a `tail -F` Monitor already watches, so no polled form is needed.

E1's gate reads "S4 or S5"; S5 satisfies it. The polled-versus-`tail -F`
comparison is therefore off the critical path.

Reopen this if the mechanization wave chooses a `git log` Monitor after all, in
which case the latency question returns.

title: Renovate bead-bonanza: eliminate, renovate, pivot to epics, mechanize, split
description:
## Context

A design review of `bead-bonanza` v1.7 found the procedure is 2.9x its own context budget (58,392 bytes against the 20,000-byte re-injection cap, so 34.3% survives a compaction), that it hand-builds in prose about eight coordination primitives `bd` already ships as commands, and that its retro loop terminates in a queue rather than an action.

This epic carries out the plan. Ordering is eliminate -> renovate -> pivot -> mechanize -> split, with spikes first because seven claims are unverified and four of them gate an elimination.

Plan: `docs/plans/bead-bonanza-renovation.md`. Review evidence: `docs/research/bead-bonanza-design/README.md`.

## Success Criteria

- [ ] Every wave epic below is closed.
- [ ] `scripts/check-skills.sh --strict` exits 0 with no warnings - the first time it has.
- [ ] The plan's delta log reads `done` on every row, and research section 1 has been reissued as a second dated snapshot.
- [ ] `docs/plans/bead-bonanza-renovation.md` is deleted, per the docs/plans convention.

## Notes

Waves 0-2 and 5 can proceed independently of each other. Wave 3 gates wave 4. Wave 6 is last by design: by then the phases have been shrunk, rewritten, restructured and partly replaced by scripts, so the split is a smaller and better-informed cut.
close_reason: All eight waves resolved. Wave 7 moved to agent-plugins-dv7q (environment-blocked: needs CLAUDE_CODE_SUBAGENT_MODEL set before a session launches). The RFC migration and the bead-bonanza -> run-sprint rename moved to agent-plugins-gzcr, both deferred so their large mechanical diffs are reviewed on their own branch rather than inside a 100+ commit PR. Everything else is closed. The full declared check set — 13 checks — passes at exit 0, including check-skills.sh --strict, which was known-red when this epic was filed.

title: Wave 2 - Renovate: replace hand-rolled procedure with bd commands and scripts
description:
## Context

Replace procedure the skill describes in prose with a `bd` command or a script. Nothing structural yet - that is wave 3. Ends by extracting the per-bead ceremony as its own skill, placed last deliberately because waves 1 and 2 both change the ceremony's content.

Plan: `docs/plans/bead-bonanza-renovation.md`. Review evidence: `docs/research/bead-bonanza-design/README.md`.

## Success Criteria

- [ ] No executable or routing fact is parsed out of markdown any more.
- [ ] Claiming, merging and the human-decision channel each use a `bd` primitive rather than a prose rule.
- [ ] The per-bead ceremony exists as an independently invocable, independently testable skill.

title: Delete the --gate-baseline flag; the baseline becomes unconditional
description:
## Context

`pre-flight-check.sh` defaults `DO_GATES=no`, but `SKILL.md`'s single canonical invocation passes `--gate-baseline` unconditionally - so it is already always-on and the flag only creates a way to get it wrong. Neither argument for opt-in survives: 'it executes arbitrary commands' is an argument about where the commands come from, answered by the checks script; 'a full suite costs ten minutes' is backwards, since a slow suite is exactly where charging a pre-existing failure to the first bead costs most. There is no opt-out either.

Plan: `docs/plans/bead-bonanza-renovation.md`. Review evidence: `docs/research/bead-bonanza-design/README.md`.

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] The `--gate-baseline` flag is removed; the baseline is always captured.
- [ ] `--self-test` still works and still takes no run id.
- [ ] The published interface in `SKILL.md` and the script header agree.
- [ ] No caller passes the flag.

title: Delete the tier: label path and its unusable bulk-query example
description:
## Context

Tier is stored twice by two skills: `groom-beads` writes it to metadata, `bead-bonanza` reads a `tier:<name>` LABEL and documents `bd list --label tier:standard --json` as a bulk query. Measured on this database: 153 beads carry `metadata.tier`, 63 carry a `tier:` label, the sets do not coincide, and the documented query returns 0 because `bd list` defaults to open issues - the same trap the findings harvest hit and fixed.

Plan: `docs/plans/bead-bonanza-renovation.md`. Review evidence: `docs/research/bead-bonanza-design/README.md`.

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] Metadata is the single home for tier; the label path is removed from `bead-bonanza`.
- [ ] The `bd list --label tier:standard --json` example is deleted, not corrected.
- [ ] Any remaining bulk query over tier is demonstrated to return a non-zero count on this database.
- [ ] `groom-beads` and `bead-bonanza` agree on one storage location.

title: Spike: is bd worktree better than raw git worktree here?
description:
## Goal

Settle, by measurement: is bd worktree better than raw git worktree here.

## Context

The bundled beads skill says to always use `bd worktree` rather than `git worktree`, because it auto-configures the beads redirect, gitignore entries and embedded mode. But bead-bonanza measured that `bd` already resolves the shared database through git's common directory from any worktree with no redirect file created - so the main stated benefit may be moot here. Its removal safety checks may still earn it.

Plan: `docs/plans/bead-bonanza-renovation.md`. Review evidence: `docs/research/bead-bonanza-design/README.md`.

## Method

- [ ] Create a worktree each way and compare what `bd where`, `bd worktree info` and the filesystem show.
- [ ] Compare `bd worktree remove` against `git worktree remove` on a dirty worktree.
- [ ] State whether N6 should adopt it, and on which of the two grounds.

## Findings

**Verdict: adopt it — but on the removal ground only. The redirect ground is
dead, and adoption carries two hazards worth handling explicitly.**

Measured on bd 1.2.2 in a scratch repo, one worktree created each way.

**The database ground is moot, as bead-bonanza measured.** `bd where` and
`bd worktree info` return identical results from both worktrees — same `.beads`
directory, same `embeddeddolt` path, and both report `Beads: local (no
redirect)`. No redirect file is created either way, and `bd worktree info`
works fine inside a worktree made by plain `git worktree add`. bd's own help now
concedes this: "Worktrees automatically share the same beads database as the
main repository via git common directory discovery — no manual redirect
configuration needed."

**The removal ground is real, and it is the whole case.** Two removal
scenarios, same setup both ways:

| worktree state | `git worktree remove` | `bd worktree remove` |
|---|---|---|
| dirty (modified + untracked) | refuses: "contains modified or untracked files, use --force" | refuses: "safety check failed: worktree has uncommitted changes" |
| **clean, 1 unpushed commit** | **removes it silently** | **refuses: "safety check failed: worktree has unpushed commits"** |

Git's own check covers only the dirty case. The clean-but-unpushed case is
exactly bead-bonanza's shape — a subagent's bead work is a *commit* on a
per-bead branch inside a worktree, so the tree is clean the moment the close
ceremony commits and before the push lands. `git worktree remove` takes that
worktree without complaint; the commit then survives only via the branch ref,
which the next cleanup step is liable to delete. `bd worktree remove` is the
only one of the two that refuses.

**Hazard 1 — it writes to the main repo's tracked `.gitignore`.**
`bd worktree create wt-bd` appended `# bd worktree` and `wt-bd/` to
`.gitignore` in the main repository. That is a tracked-file mutation per
worktree created, and bead-bonanza's close ceremony stages everything dirty in
the tree, so it would ride into the next bead's close commit unnoticed.

**Hazard 2 — a bare name nests the worktree inside the repository.**
`bd worktree create wt-bd` created `<repo>/wt-bd`, not a sibling. Hence the
`.gitignore` entry above. Adopting this means either passing an explicit path
outside the repo, or accepting the nesting plus the ignore entry.

For N6: adopt, cite removal safety as the reason, and handle both hazards in
the same change rather than inheriting them.

---

**CORRECTED 2026-08-20 while implementing the adoption bead.** The verdict above
("adopt it, on the removal ground") does not survive contact with bead-bonanza's
branch topology, and the original measurement did not test that topology.

`bd worktree remove`'s unpushed-commits check treats a branch with **no
upstream** as entirely unpushed. Measured against this repository: a worktree on
a fresh branch created from the sprint head, carrying **zero** new commits, is
refused with `safety check failed: worktree has unpushed commits`. Plain
`git worktree remove` removes the same worktree without complaint.

Every bead worktree is that shape — branched from the sprint head, never pushed
on its own, merged locally, then removed. So the check fires on every bead and
the only way through is `--force`, which skips *all* safety checks including the
dirty-tree one git still enforces on its own. Adopting it trades a real guard
for a suppressed one.

The earlier measurement used a branch that HAD diverged and HAD no upstream, so
it could not distinguish "refuses unpushed work" from "refuses any branch
without an upstream". The second reading is the correct one.

Raw `git worktree` remains correct here. The database-sharing half of this
spike is unaffected: it is identical either way.

title: A run is one epic, and admission is the step that builds it
description:
## Context

A run is a single epic. The epic id is the run id, `bd ready --parent <epic> --exclude-type=epic` is the queue, the manifest lives on the epic, and the epic is what recovery reads. Today's run id is a generated `<timestamp>-<count>` that survives only in the orchestrator's transcript.

The user does not necessarily hand over an epic — they hand over whatever they have. ADMISSION turns any input into the one epic, and it is where every measured consequence is handled.

## Admission rules

Resolve a label or priority filter to a bead set first; then:

- One epic (flat or nested) — use it. Nothing created, nothing moved. Where nested, say once that the wave preview and progress count are degraded, and NEVER flatten: flattening moves beads that have homes.
- Beads with no parent — create the run epic and adopt them.
- Beads that already belong to an epic — ASK before moving, naming which beads move and which epic each one leaves. On decline, EXCLUDE that subset from the run, record the exclusions on the epic, and name them in the report. Decline is a first-class outcome, not a failure.
- Several epics — see agent-plugins-ccm9. Whole epics are adopted intact; no bead moves.

## Measured, and not to be re-derived

- `bd ready --parent` is TRANSITIVE and includes intermediate epics, so `--exclude-type=epic` is mandatory or the run dispatches its own sub-epics as work.
- Moving a bead out of its epic makes that epic falsely report complete: a 1-closed/1-open feature epic went to `1/1 complete (100%) — eligible for close`. This is why the move is confirmed, and why there is no restore-on-completion (a crashed run would leave the lie in place).
- Membership cannot be a dependency edge. `bd dep add <epic> --depends-on <task>` fails with "epics can only block other epics, not tasks", and the reverse fails symmetrically. Non-blocking types are permitted but inert: `--type related` epic->task leaves `bd ready --parent` empty and `swarm validate` at `Total issues: 0`. Only parent-child creates membership.

Plan: docs/plans/wave-3-run-scope.md. Read it first — the measurements in it are settled and are not to be re-derived.
acceptance_criteria:
The skill resolves any input (one epic, several epics, bead ids, a label, a priority) to exactly one run epic; the epic id is used as the run id everywhere a run id appears, and the generated `<timestamp>-<count>` id is gone; the queue is `bd ready --parent <epic> --exclude-type=epic`; a move of any bead that already has a parent is confirmed with that bead's id and its current epic named, and declining excludes it from the run and records the exclusion; the "enumerate, never filter" rule is removed from every document carrying it and replaced by the delta report.

NOT this bead's: `$RUN_DIR`, the run root and the `current` symlink stay until agent-plugins-x5ix moves the manifest onto the epic — there is nowhere else for the checks baseline to live until then. This bead only changes what the directory is NAMED after.

comments.author: Claude
comments.text: measured (bd 1.2.2): `bd ready --parent <epic>` is TRANSITIVE — it returns descendants at any depth, and it INCLUDES the intermediate epic beads themselves. `bd ready --parent agent-plugins-1ilc` returned 8 rows including three wave epics alongside their grandchildren. A queue built from it must pass `--exclude-type=epic` or the run will try to dispatch its own wave epics as work.

comments.author: Claude
comments.text: measured, and it BLOCKS this bead's design: a bead has exactly ONE parent, and there is no non-destructive way to put it in a second epic. `bd dep add <bead> --type parent-child <epic>` is not an additive edge — it silently reparents, identically to `bd update --parent`. Verified on agent-plugins-7vej itself: its parent moved from agent-plugins-bir9 to a probe epic, and `bd ready --parent bir9` stopped returning it. Repaired with `bd update --parent agent-plugins-bir9`, which also cleaned up the stale dep edge; bir9's swarm validate output is identical to before the probe.

comments.author: Claude
comments.text: measured: `bd swarm validate <epic>` already produces the dependency-wave partition this wave wants — against agent-plugins-bir9 it returned Wave 1 (7vej, we2q), Wave 2 (five), Wave 3 (67xf), plus max-parallelism and a warning per cross-epic dependency edge. That is agent-plugins-205x's whole premise, confirmed before implementing against it.

comments.author: Claude
comments.text: measured: non-parent edge types do NOT create descendants. A `tracks` edge from a run epic to a bead owned by another epic left `bd ready --parent <run-epic>` empty while the bead's parent field stayed on its home epic. So 'adopt without reparenting' has no implementation — the choice is reparent or key the run on something other than an epic.

comments.author: Claude
comments.text: SCOPE CHANGED by review decision. 'A run is an epic' is rejected: it forces a project to organise its epics around runs, and it cannot express the skill's own advertised entry points (label, priority) because those cut across a hierarchy and a bead has exactly one parent. Replaced by: a run has a SELECTOR (one epic / several epics / a filter), the selector's shape decides which bd capabilities apply, and every run has a run bead carrying the manifest — which IS the epic when the selector is a single epic, and is created without owning anything otherwise. Revised plan: docs/plans/wave-3-run-scope.md.

comments.author: Claude
comments.text: measured constraints on bd swarm create: it takes exactly ONE epic, so N epics means N swarms; and given a NON-epic issue it auto-wraps by creating an epic with that issue as its only child, which is a reparent. Never point it at a bare bead.

comments.author: Claude
comments.text: measured: bd swarm status is COMPUTED from beads rather than stored ('if beads changes, status changes', per its own help, confirmed against agent-plugins-bir9 where it showed the live in-progress claim). That is what makes a live selector workable — a scope that grows between restarts is reflected without anything being re-registered.

comments.author: Claude
comments.text: measured, and it corrects a claim I made earlier in this bead: bd swarm validate and bd swarm status are ONE LEVEL DEEP. On a run epic holding one sub-epic (two leaves, one closed) plus one direct leaf, both reported Total/Progress of 2 and listed the SUB-EPIC ITSELF as a dispatchable work item; neither leaf appeared and the closed one was not counted. bd ready --parent is transitive and swarm is not — I had conflated them and written that epic-of-epics 'is measured to work'. The queue reaches through nesting; the swarm signals do not.

comments.author: Claude
comments.text: consequence: THE RUN EPIC MUST BE FLAT — its children are the beads to run. A nested run epic silently degrades the wave partition, the live view and the progress count, and would dispatch a sub-epic as if it were a bead. This is why bir9 (8 task children) validated correctly in the earlier probe while a nested epic does not.

comments.author: Claude
comments.text: DECISION (user, this session): a run is a single epic, always. The user may pass multiple beads; the skill creates the run epic itself. Where admission would MOVE a bead that already belongs to an epic, ask first — naming which beads move and which epic each leaves — and on decline EXCLUDE that subset from the run rather than moving it or refusing to run. Decline is a first-class outcome: the run proceeds with what was admitted and records the exclusions. Revised plan: docs/plans/wave-3-run-scope.md.

comments.author: Claude
comments.text: measured, and it retires the flatness requirement I recorded earlier: the re-queried ready front is correct where swarm is not. On the same graph, 'bd ready --parent <run-epic> --exclude-type=epic' after each close walked the whole DAG — a1,b2 then a2,b2 then a2 then b1 (the cross-epic edge releasing correctly) then empty. Dispatch reads the front; swarm validate's waves are a lookahead for planning and reporting, not a dispatch mechanism. Nesting therefore costs no correctness — only the wave preview and the progress count.

comments.author: Claude
comments.text: measured trap: --parent does not mean the same thing on both commands. 'bd ready --parent' returns descendants at any depth; 'bd list --parent' returns DIRECT CHILDREN ONLY — against agent-plugins-1ilc it returned 10 leaf beads for an epic with 32 descendants. A transitive progress count has to be walked. Relevant to kyyl.

comments.author: Claude
comments.text: measured: running swarm on the LEAF epics of an epic-of-epics does not rescue it — it produces WRONG answers. With a2 (in E1) blocking b1 (in E2), 'bd swarm validate E2' put b1 in Wave 1 and 'bd swarm status E2' listed it as Ready with Blocked empty. Swarm scopes dependency analysis to the epic it was given, reports the outside edge as a warning, then computes waves and readiness as if the edge were not there. Detectable, but unsafe to dispatch from.

comments.author: Claude
comments.text: measured, and it closes off the dependency-linked-run-epic idea at the tracker level: 'bd dep add <run-epic> --depends-on <task>' fails with 'epics can only block other epics, not tasks', and the reverse direction fails with 'tasks can only block other tasks, not epics'. blocks edges are type-segregated; epic<->epic and task<->task are fine, epic<->task is not. Non-blocking types are NOT segregated ('--type related' epic->task succeeds) but such an edge creates nothing: bd ready --parent returns no work and swarm validate reports Total issues: 0. Only parent-child creates membership, so the hybrid (children where free, dep-links where owned) has no implementation for its second half.

comments.author: Claude
comments.text: scope correction, caught before implementing: my own re-groomed acceptance claimed the run root and the `current` symlink, which agent-plugins-x5ix also claims. x5ix is right to own them — the run root holds the checks baseline, and it cannot be retired until the manifest has somewhere else to live. This bead retires the GENERATED run id only; the directory survives, renamed after the epic.

comments.author: Claude
comments.text: retro: nearly renamed SKILL.md's 'bd gate create -t gh:run --await-id <run-id>' during the sweep. That is a GitHub WORKFLOW run id, unrelated to a bead-bonanza run. A blind rename of the token would have silently broken the CI gate instruction.

comments.author: Claude
comments.text: retro: pre-flight now verifies the epic instead of trusting it — measured that 'bd show <unknown-id> --json' prints {"error": ...} and exits 1, so a non-empty stdout is NOT proof the bead exists. Missing and wrong-type are reported separately because they need different fixes. Without this a typo'd id would have produced an empty queue, which reads exactly like a finished run.

comments.author: Claude
comments.text: retro: the self-test asserted 'no args exits 2', which was the OLD contract. No-args is now the environment pass, so the assertion had to change with the behaviour — it now asserts that no-args is never a usage error, and adds the cases it was implicitly covering (unknown option, two epic ids).

comments.author: Claude
comments.text: retro: the epic id cannot simply replace the generated run id in pre-flight's argument, because of an ordering constraint nobody had noticed. Admission RESOLVES the epic by writing to the tracker (creating it, or reparenting into it), and pre-flight section 9 is what establishes that a closure can be pushed at all. Writing before that check is backwards. Resolved by making the epic id OPTIONAL: no argument runs the environment pass, and the epic-scoped pass follows admission. Both modes report the absence of the other's outputs rather than leaving it to be inferred.

comments.author: Claude
comments.text: retro: bead-bonanza/SKILL.md grew 57321 -> 59638 body bytes, moving the known-red size warning up. The admission rules are new required content and the old Phase 1 they replaced was much shorter, so the growth is real rather than padding — but this file is already 3x the re-injection cap and wave 6's split is what actually addresses it.

title: Spike: does bd fire an issue-level script hook on create/update/close?
description:
## Goal

Settle, by measurement: does bd fire an issue-level script hook on create/update/close.

## Context

`docs/OBSERVABILITY.md` documents a `hook.exec` span carrying `hook.event` in {create, update, close} and a `hook.path` - which would give a push signal from the tracker write itself, with no parallel file, and could supersede S4 entirely. But `docs/CONFIG.md` documents no configuration key for it and `bd config list` shows none. Note this is distinct from `bd hooks`, which manages GIT hooks.

Plan: `docs/plans/bead-bonanza-renovation.md`. Review evidence: `docs/research/bead-bonanza-design/README.md`.

## Method

- [ ] Grep the `bd` source for the hooks directory it resolves and the key that configures it.
- [ ] If a hook mechanism exists, demonstrate one firing on a `bd update`.
- [ ] State whether it can carry the live progress signal, and whether it supersedes S4.

## Findings

**Verdict: YES — and it supersedes S4.**

`bd` fires issue-level script hooks. They are undocumented in `CONFIG.md` and
absent from `bd config list` because there is **no configuration key** — the
mechanism is convention, not configuration, which is why the earlier search for
a key found nothing.

Contract, read from `internal/hooks/hooks.go` and `hooks_unix.go` at v1.2.2 and
then demonstrated:

- Path: `<workspace>/.beads/hooks/{on_create,on_update,on_close}`
  (`NewRunnerFromWorkspace` joins `.beads/hooks`).
- Must exist and be **executable**; otherwise skipped silently, no error.
- Invoked as `hook <issue_id> <event_type>` with the **full issue JSON on
  stdin**.
- Asynchronous fire-and-forget (`go func()`), timeout-bounded, killed by
  process group so descendants cannot outlive it. Hook failure never blocks the
  triggering operation. Output captured to the span, truncated at 1024 bytes.
- Emits the `hook.exec` span carrying `hook.event`, `hook.path` and
  `bd.issue_id` — which is what `OBSERVABILITY.md` documented.

Demonstrated in a scratch workspace (`bd init --prefix hk`, v1.2.2), hooks
writing to a log:

    on_create fired: id=hk-qqw event=create stdin_title=hook probe
    on_update fired: id=hk-qqw event=update stdin_title=hook probe   (--status in_progress)
    on_update fired: id=hk-qqw event=update stdin_title=hook probe   (--status closed)
    on_close  fired: id=hk-8dv event=close  stdin_title=close-path probe  (bd close)

**Trap — `on_close` does not fire on this project's own close path.**
`bd update <id> --status closed` fires `on_update` only; `on_close` fires only
for `bd close`. bead-bonanza's close ceremony uses `bd update --status closed`
deliberately, to avoid a second commit. A progress signal hung on `on_close`
would therefore never fire here. Use `on_update`, which fires on every status
change including the close.

**Consequence for E1.** The ledger's one unique property was a push signal.
`on_update` supplies it from the tracker write itself, with no parallel file
written by the subagent and no testimony involved — the hook can append the
same line a `tail -F` Monitor already watches. E1's gate ("S4 or S5") is
satisfied by this spike, so **S4 is superseded** per the plan's own
contingency.

**Hazard to carry into the mechanization wave.** `.beads/hooks/` is the same
directory bd's GIT hooks occupy, it is git-tracked in this repository, and
`bd init` rewrites its contents (observed this session: five hook scripts
rewritten unasked). An `on_update` hook installed there must be treated as
something bd may overwrite.

title: Wave 3 - The epic pivot: a run is an epic, and the epic is the queue
description:
## Context

The structural change. A run is a SINGLE EPIC: the epic id is the run id, `bd ready --parent <epic> --exclude-type=epic` is the queue, the manifest lives on the epic, and recovery reads the epic rather than a directory.

The user does not necessarily hand over an epic. ADMISSION turns whatever they gave — an epic, several epics, bead ids, a label, a priority — into that one epic, confirming any move that would take a bead out of an epic it already belongs to, and excluding rather than moving when the user declines.

Plan: docs/plans/wave-3-run-scope.md. Review evidence: docs/research/bead-bonanza-design/README.md.

## Three measurements this wave rests on

1. Dispatch reads the RE-QUERIED READY FRONT, which is dependency-correct at any depth and across epic boundaries. `bd swarm validate` is not: it scopes dependency analysis to the epic given, warns about outside edges, then computes as if they were absent — it placed a blocked bead in Wave 1. Swarm supplies a lookahead, never the dispatch order.
2. Moving a bead out of its epic makes that epic falsely report complete and eligible for close. Hence confirm-then-exclude, and no restore-on-completion.
3. Membership cannot be a dependency edge — bd refuses epic<->task `blocks` edges in both directions, and the non-blocking types it permits create no scope. Only parent-child creates membership.
acceptance_criteria: A run can be started, recovered and reported on using only an epic id; a user's input of any shape becomes exactly one run epic, with every bead move confirmed and every declined move recorded as an exclusion; $RUN_DIR holds nothing any procedure needs; dispatch order comes from the re-queried ready front rather than a stored wave table; the run reports a correct completion count on both a flat and a nested run epic.
close_reason: All eight children closed. Wave 3 delivered: a run is one epic, admission builds it, the manifest lives on the epic, dispatch reads the re-queried ready front, and the run has a computed Definition of Done.

title: Wave 0 - Spikes: settle the seven unverified claims
description:
## Context

Seven timeboxed investigations, all independent. Four of them gate an elimination in wave 1, so this wave runs first. Per D12 this wave is run BY HAND using the `bd` commands the plan intends to adopt - not via a bead-bonanza run - so it doubles as a trial of the target state.

Plan: `docs/plans/bead-bonanza-renovation.md`. Review evidence: `docs/research/bead-bonanza-design/README.md`.

## Success Criteria

- [ ] Every spike closes with a measurement in the form AGENTS.md's ledger admission rule requires: the command run, the conditions it ran under, the result observed.
- [ ] Each spike either files a follow-up bead or records an explicit 'no action'.
- [ ] Findings that change a wave-1 or wave-3 item are reflected in that bead before it starts.

title: Spike: what does CLAUDE_CODE_SUBAGENT_MODEL actually override?
description:
## Goal

Settle, by measurement: what does CLAUDE_CODE_SUBAGENT_MODEL actually override.

## Context

`SKILL.md` asserts that when this variable is set, every subagent runs at that forced model regardless of tier, so no routing occurs - and Phase 4 replaces BOTH routing tables with an `N/A` on that basis. The premise is unverified and public accounts contradict each other: one puts the env var above the per-invocation `model` parameter, another says it only affects agents without an explicit model. claude-code issue 10993 exists because the behaviour is undocumented. bead-bonanza ALWAYS passes `model:` per-invocation, so if the parameter wins, routing happens normally and Phase 4 discards two correct tables.

Plan: `docs/plans/bead-bonanza-renovation.md`. Review evidence: `docs/research/bead-bonanza-design/README.md`.

## Method

- [ ] Export the variable to a model outside the project lineup.
- [ ] Dispatch two subagents at two different resolved models via the `model` param.
- [ ] Ask each which model is serving it, and record both answers verbatim.
- [ ] State which of the two precedence rules holds, with the observed evidence.
- [ ] Record the finding so E6 can proceed or be cancelled.

## Findings

**Verdict: the premise E6 rests on is UNVERIFIED, and E6 should not proceed on it.**

What was measured. Two subagents dispatched in one session, differing only in
the per-invocation `model` parameter, each asked to report its serving model.
Serving model read from each subagent's own transcript (`"model"` field on its
assistant messages), not from self-report:

| dispatched as | model on the wire |
|---|---|
| `model: haiku` | `claude-haiku-4-5-20251001` (8 messages) |
| `model: opus`  | `claude-opus-5` (5 messages) |

So **the per-invocation `model` parameter demonstrably routes** when
`CLAUDE_CODE_SUBAGENT_MODEL` is unset. Routing happens; the tables are used.

What could NOT be measured, and why. `CLAUDE_CODE_SUBAGENT_MODEL` was `NOTSET`
in this session and in both subagents' environments, and it cannot be injected
into an already-running session — exporting it from a Bash tool call does not
reach the process that dispatches subagents. The precedence question (env var
versus `model` parameter) therefore remains open. Settling it needs the
variable set **at CLI/container launch**, then this same two-agent probe.

Consequence. `SKILL.md` asserts that when the variable is set no routing occurs,
and E6 deletes both routing tables on that basis. That assertion is now
explicitly unverified rather than merely uncited, and the half that WAS measured
cuts against it. **Do not execute E6** until the launch-time probe is run.

**Trap worth carrying — a subagent cannot learn its own model from
`get_session`.** Both probes called it and both got `session_context.model` =
`external_metadata.last_served_model` = `claude-opus-5`, because the tool
describes the parent session, not the subagent. Any check that asks a subagent
to self-report its model this way returns the orchestrator's model and looks
like a successful verification.

title: Extract the per-bead ceremony into its own skill
description:
## Context

The ceremony is a self-contained, ordered, ten-step procedure with three scripts behind it, currently living as a prose template inside `references/subagent-prompts.md` that the orchestrator is explicitly forbidden to paraphrase - a rule that exists only because the procedure has no other form. As a skill it becomes what a subagent invokes by name, what a solo agent with no Agent tool invokes directly per bead, and something independently testable, which nothing about the ceremony is today. Placed last in wave 2 deliberately: waves 1 and 2 both change the ceremony's content, so extracting earlier means editing it twice.

Plan: `docs/plans/bead-bonanza-renovation.md`. Review evidence: `docs/research/bead-bonanza-design/README.md`.

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] The ceremony exists as an invocable skill with its own acceptance criteria.
- [ ] Dispatch templates invoke it by name; the do-not-paraphrase rule is removed.
- [ ] The skill is usable standalone by an agent working one bead, with no orchestrator.
- [ ] `references/subagent-prompts.md` keeps only what is genuinely per-dispatch: the placeholders and the batch-specific steps.
- [ ] Its body is under the 20,000-byte re-injection cap.

title: Spike: does an epic-of-epics traverse for ready and swarm validate?
description:
## Goal

Settle, by measurement: does an epic-of-epics traverse for ready and swarm validate.

## Context

The multi-epic story rests on nesting: a cross-epic sprint becomes an outer epic parenting the feature epics. Nothing has confirmed that `bd ready --parent` and `bd swarm validate` reach grandchildren rather than direct children only. If they do not, P10 needs a different mechanism (`bd mol bond`, or explicit re-parenting).

Plan: `docs/plans/bead-bonanza-renovation.md`. Review evidence: `docs/research/bead-bonanza-design/README.md`.

## Method

- [ ] Run `bd ready --parent <root>` against this renovation epic and confirm it returns leaf beads, not just the seven wave epics.
- [ ] Run `bd swarm validate <root>` and confirm it analyses the full two-level graph.
- [ ] Run `bd epic status` and record how a nested epic is counted.
- [ ] State the result and, if traversal fails, name the alternative mechanism for P10.

## Notes

This spike is answered as a side effect of filing this plan's own beads, since the graph is deliberately two levels deep.

## Findings



**Answered 2026-08-20 by filing this plan's own bead graph** (root epic
`agent-plugins-1ilc`, 7 wave epics, 44 leaves — a deliberate two-level graph).

**Split verdict: one command traverses, the other does not.**

- `bd ready --parent agent-plugins-1ilc --plain` returned **12 items including
  grandchildren** (spikes under wave epics). **It traverses.** Caveat: it also
  returns the wave epics themselves, which are not workable items — add
  `--exclude-type=epic` to get the workable set (9 at the time of measurement).
- `bd swarm validate agent-plugins-1ilc` reported **"Total issues: 7 (0
  closed)"** and analysed only the seven wave epics. **It does NOT traverse** —
  it treats direct children as the work.
- Run one level down, `bd swarm validate agent-plugins-1qc8` (wave 2) correctly
  analysed that epic's 12 leaves into 3 ready fronts.

**Consequences for the plan:**

- **P4** (take dependency waves from `bd swarm validate`) must run it **per wave
  epic**, never on the sprint root. On a nested graph the root gives a useless
  answer that looks valid.
- **P8** (epic-of-epics for multi-epic runs) is viable for the *queue*
  (`ready --parent` works) but not for *wave derivation*. A cross-epic sprint
  needs `swarm validate` per member epic, and the results composed.
- The queue query wants `--exclude-type=epic` so container nodes are not
  dispatched as work.
close_reason: Answered by filing the renovation graph: ready --parent traverses two levels, swarm validate does not.

title: Replace gate-profile prose parsing with a project checks script
description:
## Context

Pre-flight parses executable commands out of `AGENTS.md` markdown bullets with awk, plus a documented rule about which bullets are commands and which are commentary, then runs `bash -c` on each. It is the most fragile step in the pre-flight and the reason `--gate-baseline` was ever opt-in. A project-supplied `checks` script gives one known entry point the project commits and owns. title: Spike: what do event beads, set-state and metadata cost at run volume?
description:
## Goal

Settle, by measurement: what do event beads, set-state and metadata cost at run volume.

## Context

Three storage decisions depend on this: the subagent dispatch record (D2, two event beads per dispatch), the health watchdog (`bd set-state <id> health=...`), and the manifest on the epic (D9, `--metadata` JSON). None has been measured, and `bd create --graph` types metadata as map[string]string, so array-valued metadata cannot go through the graph format at all.

Plan: `docs/plans/bead-bonanza-renovation.md`. Review evidence: `docs/research/bead-bonanza-design/README.md`.

## Method

- [ ] Write 100 event beads against a scratch bead; time `bd dolt push` before and after.
- [ ] Run the eight phase transitions via `bd set-state` and record label churn.
- [ ] Establish whether `bd` bounds metadata size, and whether `--metadata` round-trips a nested object set via `bd update`.
- [ ] `bd delete` the scratch beads and confirm `bd doctor --check=pollution` is clean.
- [ ] Record all four results; state which of D2, D9 and M5 they support or refute.

## Findings

**Verdict: D9 and M5 are cheap and supported. D2 is the expensive one — and
its cost does not go away when the beads do.**

Measured on bd 1.2.2 in a scratch workspace with a local Dolt remote
(`git+file://` — accepted, so push timing is measurable without touching the
real tracker). Absolute times are local-remote times; the ratios are the
finding.

**1. Event beads — 100 written against one target bead.**

| | cost |
|---|---|
| writing 100 `--type event` beads | 67.8s (0.68s each, sequential) |
| `bd dolt push`, before | 0.63s |
| `bd dolt push`, after | **5.36s (8.5x)** |
| `bd delete` of all 101 | 12.5s |
| `bd dolt push`, after deletion | **1.56s — still 2.5x the original baseline** |

Deleting the beads did not restore the baseline. Dolt is versioned: the writes
remain in the commit graph, so the weight an event bead adds to the tracker is
permanent even after the bead is gone. D2 proposes **two event beads per
dispatch**; a 12-bead wave is 24 event beads, and that cost accrues to every
future clone and bootstrap, not just to the run that wrote them. Combined with
S7's finding that tracker writes serialize globally, D2 is the most expensive
proposal of the three by a wide margin. It needs a per-run volume budget or a
cheaper carrier.

**2. `bd set-state` — supported, and it does NOT churn.** Eight phase
transitions on one bead took 5.1s (0.64s each). It is implemented as a label
that **replaces** rather than accumulates: after all eight, the bead carried
exactly one label, `phase:reported`. One current value, queryable by label, no
history litter. M5 is cheap and behaves correctly.

**3. Metadata — larger and richer than the graph format suggested.**
`bd update --metadata` accepts **nested objects and arrays** and round-trips
them intact (`{"manifest":{"waves":[1,2,3],"owner":"orch"}}` came back as a
real dict containing a real array). Successive `--metadata` calls **merge**
rather than replace — three separate writes left all three keys present. No
size bound was hit: a single 100,000-character value was accepted and read back
at full length.

This reconciles the concern in this bead's context. `bd create --graph` types
metadata as `map[string]string`, so arrays genuinely cannot pass **through the
graph format** — but that is a limitation of the graph importer, not of
metadata. D9's manifest is fully supported provided it is written with
`bd update --metadata` after the graph is applied, rather than inside the graph
file.

**4. `bd doctor` is unavailable here.** `bd doctor --check=pollution` returns
"'bd doctor' is not yet supported in embedded mode" — and this project runs
embedded. Cleanup was verified with `bd list` instead: 1 task remaining, 0
event beads. Any future design step that leans on `bd doctor` for a health or
pollution check will not run in this repository.

title: Attach the run manifest to the run epic; retire $RUN_DIR
description:
## Context

Per D9 the plan splits into a derived part and a recorded part. The wave table is DERIVED — recomputable from the graph — so storing it only creates drift. What is not derivable is the manifest (checks baseline, model lineup, effort, standing authorization, environmental ledger, base sha, the admission record including any excluded beads) and the amendments log.

The run epic is where both go, which empties $RUN_DIR entirely.

## Depends on the admission rules in agent-plugins-7vej

The manifest must record what admission decided: which beads were admitted, which were excluded and why, and whether any bead was moved (with its previous parent), so recovery and the final report can both state it without re-deriving it.

Plan: docs/plans/wave-3-run-scope.md. Read it first — the measurements in it are settled and are not to be re-derived.
acceptance_criteria: The manifest is `--metadata` JSON on the run epic and `bd show <epic> --json | jq .metadata` retrieves it whole; amendments are `amend:`-prefixed comments on the epic, append-only and timestamped by construction; the admission record (admitted / excluded / moved-from) is part of the manifest; the wave table is not stored; trailers move to the epic and the session is recorded with `bd update <id> --session`; `$RUN_DIR`, the run root and `dispatch.md` are retired; recover-sprint reads the epic, not a directory.

comments.author: Claude
comments.text: measured before designing: a 4 KB manifest with a multi-KB checks baseline embedded round-trips through 'bd update --metadata' byte-identically, and nested structures (the excluded list of {id, reason} objects) survive. --metadata also accepts @file.json, which is how a large manifest gets written without shell quoting. That is what made moving the baseline off disk viable rather than hopeful.

comments.author: Claude
comments.text: retro: --trailers-file could not simply be re-pointed, because the trailers stopped being a file. Added --trailers-from <epic> to bb-close-bead.sh, which reads .metadata.trailers and materialises a temp file behind the existing code path, and made the two flags mutually exclusive. Exercised all four paths by hand (both flags, epic without trailers, unknown epic, epic with trailers) since that script has no self-test — filing that gap is worth doing.

comments.author: Claude
comments.text: retro: plan-sprint's OUT contract shrank from two things to one. It used to write the wave table to dispatch.md AND return it; with the table derivable from the graph, writing it could only produce drift. references/dispatch-plan.md was renamed references/run-record.md because it now documents the manifest's JSON shape on the epic, not a markdown file's layout — a stale filename is the residue pattern this review keeps finding.

comments.author: Claude
comments.text: retro: the merge-not-replace rule is load-bearing and was nearly missed. pre-flight writes the baseline into the SAME metadata object that grooming's keys (plan, tier, est_size) and admission's record live in, so a bare --metadata write would silently delete them. Verified against a real epic: after pre-flight wrote three baseline keys, plan/tier/est_size/tier_reason were all still present.

comments.author: Claude
comments.text: retro: recover-sprint needed more than a source swap. Its step 1 was 'find the run directory, and never guess it from mtimes' — advice about a hazard that no longer exists. Replaced with finding the epic (bd swarm list, checking each molecule's own status because closed ones list as Active; else git log plus bd show), and step 2 now re-derives the queue and REPORTS THE DELTA against the manifest's admitted list rather than treating a stored enumeration as the plan.

title: Spike: does embedded Dolt contend under concurrent subagents?
description:
## Goal

Settle, by measurement: does embedded Dolt contend under concurrent subagents.

## Context

Beads' documented default storage mode is embedded: single-writer, file-locked; multi-writer needs an external `dolt sql-server`. Concurrent worktree subagents each run `bd update`, `bd comment` and `bd dolt push` against one database. Five runs have reported no lock failure, so this may be fine at 2-4 agents - but nothing has measured it, and every proposal that adds tracker writes (D2, M5) makes it worse.

Plan: `docs/plans/bead-bonanza-renovation.md`. Review evidence: `docs/research/bead-bonanza-design/README.md`.

## Method

- [ ] Dispatch a concurrent wave with `BD_OTEL_STDOUT=true`.
- [ ] Read `bd_db_lock_wait_ms` and `bd_db_retry_count_total` and record the distribution.
- [ ] State the concurrency ceiling this implies, and whether D2 and M5 change it.

## Findings

**Verdict: it does not fail, it SERIALIZES. The ceiling is throughput, not
errors — and that changes what D2 and M5 cost.**

Measured on bd 1.2.2, embedded Dolt, a scratch workspace (`bd init --prefix
cnt`) on a 4-CPU container. N concurrent writer processes against one database,
each doing 3 `bd update --notes` plus 3 `bd comment` (6 writes per writer):

| writers | wall | writes | writes/sec | hard failures |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 1.7s | 6 | 3.53 | 0 |
| 2 | 3.0s | 12 | 4.00 | 0 |
| 4 | 6.7s | 24 | 3.58 | 0 |
| 8 | 14.7s | 48 | 3.27 | 0 |

**Zero lock failures, zero retries surfaced, zero error text at every level.**
The single-writer file lock queues writers rather than rejecting them, so the
"five runs reported no lock failure" observation is real and will keep being
real — it is not evidence of headroom.

**Throughput is flat.** Wall time scales linearly with writer count while
writes/sec stays at 3.3-4.0 throughout. At 2 and 4 writers — at or below the
4-core count, so CPU saturation is not the explanation — four concurrent
writers achieve the same aggregate throughput as one, and each individual
writer takes 4x as long to finish its own work. Serialization, not parallelism.
The 8-writer row is confounded by having only 4 cores and should not be read as
a separate data point.

**What this costs D2 and M5.** A tracker write is ~0.28s of *globally
exclusive* time, and every subagent's writes queue behind every other's. D2's
two event beads per dispatch and M5's per-phase `set-state` writes are not
free-and-parallel; they are additions to one serial queue shared by the whole
wave. A wave of 4 subagents each making 10 tracker writes is ~40 serialized
writes, ~11s of wall time that no amount of concurrency removes, plus the
latency each agent waits through. Budget tracker writes per bead, and prefer
one write carrying several facts over several writes carrying one each.

**Instrumentation note — the method in this spike's plan does not work.** The
metric names are `bd.db.lock_wait_ms` and `bd.db.retry_count` (dots, not the
underscores this bead assumed), they are registered in
`internal/storage/dolt/store.go`, and `BD_OTEL_STDOUT=true` does **not** emit
them: it emits *traces*. One `bd update` produced 1.6 MB / 95,791 lines of
pretty-printed spans, overwhelmingly `nbs.Get` from Dolt's block store. Reading
the metrics needs an OTLP collector via `BD_OTEL_METRICS_URL`. `BD_OTEL_STDOUT`
is unusable for live run observation at this volume. The outcome measurement
above is stronger evidence than the metric would have been anyway.

title: Delete the per-bead handoff file; fold its caveat onto the bead
description:
## Context

Measured across run 1786345424-bbh: the handoff file was written 23 times and needed ONCE - on the one bead that crashed, where it was ABSENT, because the agent died between emitting `retro-written` and writing the file. The close ceremony now writes a minimal one itself when none exists, so the file is produced by the ceremony anyway, and its entire remaining payload is one `Caveat:` line that is `none` in the overwhelming majority of cases.
