[ ] The claim that regenerate-cli-snapshots.sh rewrites both artifacts is re-measured before the text is committed, per AGENTS.md's rule that a tool claim binds where it is run
[ ] scripts/ci.sh passes

title: Record that the reference-property derivation is keyed on a schema definition's name
description:
Approved as rfc-0025 P1 by the repository owner in review of PR #38.

specs/modules/spec-profile/spec-profile-module.md describes the derivation accurately and says nothing about what breaks it. A reader learns that the registration is derived; they do not learn it is derived by MATCHING ONE DEFINITION'S NAME, so renaming that definition silently empties the registration for every document type.

This is not hypothetical: run agent-plugins-59ic hit it. Bead agent-plugins-rc14.2 retyped reference-bearing frontmatter properties to a new Citation alias, which silently broke the whole profile registration — every check run failed with config/invalid-registration — until cli/profile/registration.go was retargeted.

Add one sentence to that paragraph, immediately after the sentence beginning 'cli/profile/registration.go reads the reference properties…':

> The match is on the definition's name — #/definitions/Citation in the decoded schema — so renaming or replacing that definition in schemas/vocabulary.strata empties every type's registration until this file is retargeted with it, and corpus.ValidateRegistration reports the result as a fatal config/invalid-registration rather than as a missing reference.

Backward compatibility: documentation only; no document or code becomes invalid.
acceptance_criteria:
[ ] The sentence above is added to spec-profile-module.md's derivation paragraph, in the position stated
[ ] scripts/ci.sh passes

title: AGENTS.md's cli/** coverage rule needs a concurrent-run exception
description:
AGENTS.md ("Checks") states that a change under cli/** "is therefore not
finished until that script has been run from the repository root and the README
diff committed with it." Under a CONCURRENT swarm run that instruction is
wrong: each dispatch regenerates the same generated table from a different
tree, so two dispatches produce two different correct-for-their-tree tables and
neither is correct for the merge.

The rule needs a concurrent-run exception. It does not need moving to CI.

## Why "put it in CI" is already answered, and refused

Measured on this tree, .github/workflows/cli.yml lines 135-140:

  # --check measures, then fails if README.md does not already say
  # what was measured. The alternative — a job that commits the
  # regenerated README — would put the number outside review, which
  # is where an unnoticed coverage drop lives.
  - name: Measure coverage and verify the README is current
    run: scripts/coverage.sh --check

So a coverage job already exists, it already gates on --check, and the
alternative of having CI commit the regenerated README is explicitly rejected
with a reason that holds. This bead must not undo that. The --check gate stays
exactly as it is.

## What it cost, measured on run agent-plugins-59ic

Recorded by the run's coordinator as an `amend:` comment on run epic
agent-plugins-59ic:

  "rebasing dev-59ic-a onto sprint conflicted in README.md — the generated
  coverage table. Both dev-59ic-a and dev-59ic-c regenerate it, so a textual
  resolution would have committed figures matching neither tree. Resolved by
  taking the incoming side to complete the rebase, then re-running
  scripts/coverage.sh on the combined tree (2,870/3,202 = 89.6%) and folding
  the result into rc14.4's commit, which already carried a coverage update.
  Full check suite re-run on the rebased tree: exit 0."

NEITHER SIDE OF THE CONFLICT WAS CORRECT. That is the shape of the defect: it
is not a merge conflict to be resolved, it is two measurements of two different
trees, one of which is the tree that will actually ship.

## Recurrence: 1

Run agent-plugins-d7w5 (2026-09-04) pre-empted exactly this by hand. Its beads'
Design sections and its dispatch prompt carried: "DO NOT run
scripts/coverage.sh or commit README.md coverage figures. The run's coordinator
regenerates coverage once at the end." Three separate beads recorded complying
with it (findings d7w5.7#3, d7w5.8#4, d7w5.9#3, quoted in
docs/retros/2026-09-04-d7w5-spec-corpus-structure-extraction.md), one of them
naming the reason: "Rejected alternative: regenerate per bead — it would
guarantee a README.md merge conflict with the sibling batch, which is why the
instruction exists."

A remedy that has to be re-invented per bead, per run, and that the very next
run did not carry, belongs in the standing instruction instead.

## Done is

AGENTS.md's "Checks" section carries the exception beside the rule: coverage is
regenerated ONCE PER RUN, by the coordinator, on the merged tree — no bead
under a concurrent run runs scripts/coverage.sh or commits README.md coverage
figures. The CI --check gate in .github/workflows/cli.yml is untouched, and the
comment above it quoted here stays. A run's beads then need no per-bead
instruction to avoid the conflict, and grooming does not have to stamp one into
each of them.

## Anchors

The quoted sentence in AGENTS.md under "## Checks"; the coverage job and its
comment in .github/workflows/cli.yml; scripts/coverage.sh; the run epic
agent-plugins-59ic's amend: comment quoted above;
docs/retros/2026-09-05-59ic-spec-corpus-anchor-references.md and
docs/retros/2026-09-04-d7w5-spec-corpus-structure-extraction.md.

Filed by the retro of run agent-plugins-59ic.

title: The feature-blueprint template does not require a delta to list consumers that resolve a declaration by name
description:
plugin/skills/spec/references/feature-blueprint-template.md tells a delta to
list its Anchors and does not say that a delta which RENAMES or RETYPES a
declaration must list every consumer that resolves that declaration BY NAME —
a JSON-schema `$ref` match, a string literal, a reflection key — and not only
the files that declare it.

## What it cost, measured on run agent-plugins-59ic

Finding rc14.2#1, recorded in flight on agent-plugins-rc14.2:

  "The bead's Design/AC list named schemas/vocabulary.strata,
  schemas/frontmatter.strata and scripts/generate-schemas.sh as the anchors,
  but retyping every reference-bearing property from Slug to Citation silently
  broke cli/profile/registration.go's derivation, which auto-registers
  reference-bearing properties by matching the JSON schema $ref
  "#/definitions/Slug". After the retype nothing matched, so every document
  type's ReferenceProperties came back empty, which
  cli/core/corpus.ValidateRegistration then reported as a fatal
  config/invalid-registration error at check time (measured: 'profile
  registration: "feature-blueprint.frd" is registered as a typed reference but
  not as a reference-bearing property') — the corpus checker was completely
  broken until this was found and fixed."

The SREF delta's Anchors line reads, in full: "`schemas/vocabulary.strata` (the
`Slug` alias), `schemas/frontmatter.strata` (the reference-bearing
properties), `scripts/generate-schemas.sh`." It names three files and not
cli/profile/registration.go. This was the most expensive single failure of the
run.

## Why this is the project's, and not somebody else's

rfc-0025 (rfcs/inbox/feature-blueprint/rfc-0025-implementing-anchor-references.md)
fixes the INSTANCE as its P1 — one sentence added to module-spec-profile — and
explicitly declines the durable form, routing it under "Considered and Not
Proposed":

  "The durable form of this is a constraint on the feature-blueprint TEMPLATE
  — 'a delta that renames a declaration lists every consumer that names it' —
  which lands in the repository that vends the template, not in this project's
  documents. Routed to the skill lens; P1 takes only the half that lands here."

THAT REPOSITORY IS THIS ONE. plugin/skills/spec/references/feature-blueprint-template.md
is in this tree, and agent-plugins-im99 is an open bead against that same file.
The rule that would have prevented the run's worst failure was therefore routed
out of the project and filed nowhere at all. The run's retro
(docs/retros/2026-09-05-59ic-spec-corpus-anchor-references.md, "Routing")
records the mis-route.

## Done is

The feature-blueprint template's delta guidance says that a delta renaming or
retyping a declaration lists, in its Anchors, every consumer that resolves it
by name — schema `$ref` matches, string literals, reflection keys — not only
the files that declare it. scripts/check-template-drift.py and
scripts/check-skills.sh stay green. It is a template edit, so no hand-authored
copy needs editing; re-run scripts/sync-shared-references.sh if a vendored copy
carries it.

## Anchors

plugin/skills/spec/references/feature-blueprint-template.md (its delta /
Anchors guidance); the quoted "Considered and Not Proposed" bullet in

title: The CLI guide still says anchors are split off, not resolved, and names four reference rules
description:
`specs/guides/spec-cli-reference.md` documents the CLI's reference checking as
it behaved at `base_sha`, and this run changed that behaviour without touching
the guide. It now states the OPPOSITE of what the tool does, and the falsity is
propagated to the vendored copy shipped with the `spec` skill.

The guide is NOT in this run's diff: `git diff --name-only 225751e...HEAD |
grep -i spec-cli-reference` returns nothing.

## The false claims, quoted

Under "Reference checks":

> `spec check` applies four rules to references. All four resolve a
> reference against the target's frontmatter `slug`, never a file path,
> and without regard to letter case.

and in the list below it:

> - **An anchor is split off, not resolved.** `[[container-x#Some
>   Heading]]` resolves on `container-x` alone; whether that document has
>   such a heading is not asked, and no finding is raised about the anchor.

and below that:

> **`spec check <path>` reports the reference findings your edit caused
> elsewhere.** All four reference rules escape the narrowing to the file
> you name

## Measured contradiction

Binary built from `cli/` on this branch (a852925). A corpus with
`[[adr-700-noheads#Ghost]]` citing a member that has no such heading:

    docs/adrs/adr-800-current.md:
      reference/unresolved-anchor  error  12:7  no heading named "Ghost" in docs/adrs/adr-700-noheads.md

So a finding IS raised about the anchor, and it is resolved against headings
rather than against the target's `slug`. The same run's `checks:` roll-up lists
SIX reference rules, not four:

    reference/ambiguous-anchor
    reference/pairing-incomplete
    reference/retired-target
    reference/type-mismatch
    reference/unresolved
    reference/unresolved-anchor

The rule table in the guide lists only four and names neither anchor rule.

## The `spec refs` paragraph is stale too

The guide says:

> By default it lists every corpus member whose body or reference-bearing
> frontmatter names that slug, each at the line and column of the reference
> ... `--json` emits each reference with its path, span, origin (body or
> which frontmatter property) and what it resolved to

Measured, the DEFAULT output is now YAML already carrying all of that:

    slug: adr-700-noheads
    direction: inbound
    declared: true
    references:
      - path: docs/adrs/adr-800-current.md
        text: adr-700-noheads#Ghost
        slug: adr-700-noheads
        anchor: Ghost
        origin:
          kind: body
        position:
          offset: 215
          ...
        resolution:
          state: resolved
          target_path: docs/adrs/adr-700-noheads.md

The anchor-qualified query form this run shipped — `spec refs
'<slug>#<Heading>'` — is not documented in the guide at all.

## One defect, one remedy — not two

`plugin/skills/spec/references/shared/spec-cli-reference.md` carries every one
of these claims verbatim, but it is GENERATED, not hand-authored:
`scripts/sync-shared-references.sh` maps `spec` to
`specs/guides/spec-cli-reference.md`. `./scripts/sync-shared-references.sh
--check` exits 0 ("all 27 vendored references are current"), so the copy is
faithful and the source is what is wrong. Fixing the guide and re-running the
sync script fixes both; editing the vendored copy directly would be reverted.

This matters because that vendored copy is exported into other projects with
the `spec` skill, where it is the only description of the CLI a reader has —
the surface `AGENTS.md` names as the hardest to reach with a correction.

## Origin

Not attributable to one bead. The two anchor rules arrive in
`agent-plugins-rc14.4` and `agent-plugins-rc14.6`; the `refs` output shape and
the anchor-qualified query in `agent-plugins-rc14.7`. Parented to the run epic
for that reason.

Filed by review pass 1 of run agent-plugins-59ic.

title: renderYAML ignores encoding/json's `omitzero`, so a key present in one rendering is absent from the other
description:
## Problem

`typeFields` in `cli/cmd/yaml.go` reads exactly one option off the json
tag:

    omitEmpty: opts["omitempty"],

Go 1.24 — the toolchain this module pins in `cli/go.mod` (`go 1.24`) —
also honours `omitzero`, which omits a field whose value is the zero value
for its type. `renderYAML` does not, so a field tagged `omitzero` appears
as a KEY in the YAML rendering and not in the JSON one.

This is the same class as agent-plugins-zka9 (`,string`) but a strictly
worse one: zka9 is a divergence in a value's TYPE, this is a divergence in
whether the KEY EXISTS. zka9's own description asserts as settled premise
that "the two renderings now carry the same KEYS in the same order" — that
premise is false while `omitzero` is unhandled.

## Measured

go1.24.7, probe run against HEAD (`62e9e42`) in package `cmd`:

    v := struct {
        A string    `json:"a,omitzero"`
        T time.Time `json:"t,omitzero"`
        B string    `json:"b"`
    }{"", time.Time{}, "y"}

    JSON: {"b":"y"}
    YAML: a: ""
          t: {}
          b: y

Three keys where JSON writes one.

## Why it matters beyond the code

`specs/containers/spec-cli/spec-cli-container.md` gained this sentence in
the same commit that shipped the fix (b9b9510):

  "so the two renderings carry the same keys in the same order and neither
  can quietly gain or lose a value the other has"

That is a universal, and `omitzero` falsifies it. The bead this came from
(d7w5.11) existed precisely because the PREVIOUS universal in that document
("cannot drift into carrying different values") was false. Replacing one
false universal with another is the defect repeating rather than closing.

## Why the guard did not catch it

`cli/cmd/yaml_promotion_test.go` is a hand-written table of struct shapes.
It is genuinely differential — it compares against `encoding/json`'s real
output rather than a hand-written expectation, verified — but it can only
catch a shape somebody thought to write down, and no case carries
`omitzero`. It does not scan the real result types on the command surface,
so the first field tagged `omitzero` will drift without failing a test.

## Why it is latent

Nothing in the tree uses it. Measured:

    $ grep -rn 'omitzero\|,string"' --include=*.go cli/ | grep -v _test.go
    (no output)

## Suggested shape

Either honour `omitzero` in `typeFields`/`structFields` (it needs the
`IsZero()`-method handling `encoding/json` does, not just `reflect.IsZero`),
or narrow the container document's sentence to the options actually
reproduced and have `cli-output-standards` forbid the rest on this surface
— the same choice zka9 offers. Decide both together; they are one question.

title: renderYAML re-resolves a struct's field set for every VALUE, making the YAML rendering 1.75x slower than before d7w5.11
description:
## Problem

agent-plugins-d7w5.11 replaced `structFields` in `cli/cmd/yaml.go` with a
port of `encoding/json`'s `typeFields`. The port is faithful, but it drops
the one thing `encoding/json` does around it: `encoding/json` memoizes the
resolved field set per `reflect.Type` in a `sync.Map` (`cachedTypeFields`)
precisely because resolving it is expensive. This port re-resolves the
whole type for every struct VALUE rendered.

It is then paid twice per value. `writeYAMLValue` calls `structFields`, and
`isBlock` calls it again for the same value:

    case reflect.Struct:
        return len(structFields(v)) > 0

## Measured

Benchmark on a `headingsResult` of 2,434 `headingMatch` entries — the size
of this repository's own corpus, i.e. `spec headings` with no selection —
20 iterations, same container, go1.24.7:

    ec6b6fd (before):  22,705,641 ns/op  10,507,047 B/op  130,969 allocs/op
    HEAD    (after):   39,840,072 ns/op  17,541,522 B/op  211,325 allocs/op

1.75x slower, 1.67x more memory, 1.61x more allocations.

## Why it matters

AC-SPEC-009.1 in `specs/features/spec-index/spec-index-frd.md` states the
target for "a corpus query against a warm index" as 50 milliseconds. The
YAML RENDERING alone now costs 39.8 ms of that budget on this corpus,
before the query itself. The container document
`specs/containers/spec-cli/spec-cli-container.md` names `spec headings` as
"exactly the corpus query FEAT-SPEC-009.1's latency budget is measured
against".

The target is explicitly a target and not a gate, and the figure above is
from a 4-core container rather than a reference environment — so treat the
1.75x ratio as the durable fact and the absolute number as indicative.

## Suggested shape

Memoize `typeFields` per `reflect.Type`, as `encoding/json` does. Prototyped
on a scratch copy of HEAD (a package-level `sync.Map`, load-or-compute):

    memoized:          14,747,605 ns/op   7,857,201 B/op   48,199 allocs/op

That is 2.7x faster than HEAD and faster than the pre-change code, with the
shipped differential suite still passing. Having `writeYAMLMapping` reuse
the slice it was handed instead of letting `isBlock` recompute is the
complementary half.

## Measured during cause investigation (see comments for invocations)

Facts only; nothing here selects a remedy.

- **Reproduced** from `git archive` trees at `ec6b6fd` and `62e9e42`,
  go1.24.7, one identical benchmark in each, both rendering byte-identical
  output (sha256 `1088869c...`): 25.1M -> 45.6M ns/op, 133,021 ->
  213,370 allocs/op. 1.81x, +80,349 allocs.
- **Resolution count is 3n+1** in corpus entries, over **3 distinct
  types** at every size (`headingsResult`, `headingMatch`, `Span`).
  7,303 calls at n=2,434. Cost is per VALUE and linear in corpus size;
  the information computed is O(1).
- **`Span` is resolved twice per entry** (`isBlock` at yaml.go:133 and
  `writeYAMLValue` at yaml.go:64); `headingMatch` is resolved once,
  because sequence entries never reach `isBlock`.
- **Per-value resolution and the double call BOTH predate d7w5.11.** In
  the pre-change tree `isBlock` already carried 31.17% of allocations.
  Neither is new; they are the multiplier, not the change.
- **What changed is the fixed cost of one resolution: +11 allocations,**
  identical for a 5-field and a 6-field type, so it is not per field.
  80,349 / 7,303 = 11.00. Of the 11, **6 are the two `sort.Slice` calls**
  (measured: 3.00 allocs each via `internal/reflectlite.Swapper`; a
  diagnostic build with an allocation-free sort drops allocs/op to
  169,554, exactly -6.00 per resolution) and ~4 are the `visited` map,
  the `nextCount` map and the `next` slice. Per-field tag handling is a
  wash between the two versions.
- **The BFS walk itself costs nothing for these types** — neither has an
  embedded field, so the loop runs one round. The expense is the
  scaffolding allocated to be able to walk.
- **`spec headings` with no operand returns 609 matches on this
  repository, not 2,434** (measured with binaries from both trees; the
  index carries 609 headings). The "Measured" section above and its
  AC-SPEC-009.1 comparison rest on 2,434 and have not been reproduced at
  that size. At n=609 the rendering is 5.3 ms before / 9.4 ms after, and
  the whole command is 97.1 ms before / 102.2 ms after (median of 7 warm
  runs, 4-core Xeon @2.10GHz container).
- **`renderYAML` has one non-test caller**, `cmd/headings.go:243`.
- **The memo prototype's advantage over the PRE-change code is real and
  explained:** two thirds of the pre-change renderer's allocations
  (`jsonName` cum 67.16%) were re-parsing constant json tags per field
  per value — `strings.Split` plus a `map[string]bool`. Both versions
  recompute a per-type answer per value; d7w5.11 made each
  recomputation dearer without introducing the recomputation.

comments.author: coordinator-d7w5
comments.text:
## Cause investigation, pass 1 of 5 — REPRODUCTION

Reproduced. Scratch trees only; nothing under cli/ was touched.

Setup — `git archive ec6b6fd | tar -x -C $S/before`, same for `62e9e42`
into `$S/after`; one identical benchmark file dropped into each
`cli/cmd/`, rendering a `headingsResult` of 2,434 synthetic
`headingMatch` entries. go1.24.7, Intel Xeon @2.10GHz, 4 cores.

Both trees render BYTE-IDENTICAL output for the corpus, so this is a
like-for-like comparison and not two different documents:

    $ go test ./cmd -run TestYztvDump -v | grep YZTV
    before: YZTV len=708661 sha256=1088869c4f85fda691db1375c93984766acf58c46feee252870fbbfd9880915e
    after:  YZTV len=708661 sha256=1088869c4f85fda691db1375c93984766acf58c46feee252870fbbfd9880915e

    $ go test ./cmd -run '^$' -bench BenchmarkYztvRenderYAML -benchtime 20x -count 3 -benchmem

    before (ec6b6fd)   25595150 / 24833031 / 25076767 ns/op
                       11454476 / 11454144 / 11453944 B/op
                         133023 /   133022 /   133020 allocs/op

    after  (62e9e42)   44860871 / 47186250 / 44668112 ns/op
                       18487025 / 18486728 / 18486293 B/op
                         213372 /   213371 /   213368 allocs/op

1.81x slower, 1.61x more bytes, **+80,349 allocs/op** — the retro's
figures reproduce, including its +80k allocation delta. A second run of
the same command a few minutes later gave before 22.3-22.9 M and after
38.2-45.5 M; the ratio is stable, the absolute ns/op moves ~10% run to
run on this container.

`cli/` at HEAD (892b9b7) is identical to 62e9e42 — `git diff --stat
62e9e42..892b9b7 -- cli/` is empty — so the "after" tree is current code.

comments.author: coordinator-d7w5
comments.text:
## Pass 2 of 5 — MECHANISM. The bead's two claims are both true and
## NEITHER of them is the cause.

### Call counts, measured not reasoned

A copy of the after tree with a counter at the head of `typeFields` and
`structFields`, over the same 2,434-entry corpus:

    typeFields cmd.headingsResult        1
    typeFields cmd.headingMatch       2434
    typeFields specmodel.Span         4868
    TOTAL 7303 calls over 3 DISTINCT TYPES

So both hypotheses on the bead hold: resolution is per VALUE (2,434
resolutions of one type), and `Span` is resolved TWICE per entry (4,868 =
2 x 2,434) — once by `isBlock` at yaml.go:133 and once by
`writeYAMLValue` at yaml.go:64. `headingMatch` is NOT double-resolved:
sequence entries reach `writeYAMLValue` through `writeYAMLSequence`,
which never calls `isBlock`. The doubling applies only to a struct
appearing as a MAPPING VALUE.

### But both of those predate d7w5.11

The pre-change tree resolves per value too, and its `isBlock` calls
`structFields` too. Its own alloc profile shows it:

    $ go tool pprof -sample_index=alloc_objects -top   (before tree)
      2162786 36.04%  cmd.jsonName
      1867803 31.12%  strings.genSplit
      1415248 23.58%  cmd.structFields
            0     0%  cmd.isBlock            cum 1870616  31.17%

`isBlock` already carried 31% of allocations BEFORE the change. Neither
per-value resolution nor the double call is new. They are the MULTIPLIER
the regression is paid through, not the regression.

### What actually changed: the fixed cost of ONE resolution

`testing.AllocsPerRun` on `structFields` for the two live types:

              headingMatch   Span
    before         15         17
    after          26         28
    delta         +11        +11

+11 in both — identical for a 5-field type and a 6-field type, so the new
cost is NOT per field. Per field the two versions are a wash: the old
`jsonName` did `strings.Split(tag, ",")` (1 alloc) + `opts :=
map[string]bool{}` (1); the new code does `index := make([]int, ...)` (1)
+ `parseJSONTag`'s opts map (1).

The +11 is FIXED SCAFFOLDING that `typeFields` sets up per call, and the
arithmetic closes exactly:

    80,349 measured delta / 7,303 resolutions = 11.00 allocs per resolution

Line-level attribution inside `typeFields` (after tree, alloc_objects,
7.30M of 9.38M total objects = 77.8% cum):

    305847   L394  count, nextCount = nextCount, map[reflect.Type]int{}
    2119092  L426  name, opts := parseJSONTag(tag)
    1245202  L431  index := make([]int, len(e.index)+1)
    1476165  L445  fields = append(fields, fieldSpec{...})
    1048610  L472  sort.Slice(fields, func(i, j int) bool {   [dominance sort]
    1103229  L504  sort.Slice(fields, ... lessByIndex ...)    [declaration order]

Of the +11, **6 are the two `sort.Slice` calls**. Measured two ways:

  - `testing.AllocsPerRun` on `sort.Slice` over a 6-element `[]fieldSpec`
    = **3.00 allocs** (internal/reflectlite.Swapper's temp plus the
    interface boxing). Two calls = 6.
  - A diagnostic variant of the after tree with the two `sort.Slice`
    calls replaced by an allocation-free insertion sort — same bytes out
    (sha256 1088869c...), full `go test ./cmd` green — drops allocs/op
    from 213,371 to **169,554**, i.e. −43,817 = **6.00 per resolution**,
    and ns/op from ~41.2M to ~33.2M.

The remaining ~4 are `visited` (map), `nextCount` (map) and `next`
(slice): measured together at 4 allocs.

### The BFS walk itself costs nothing here

Neither `headingMatch` nor `Span` has an embedded field, so `next` is
empty after round one and the loop runs exactly once. The expense is the
scaffolding `typeFields` allocates to be ABLE to walk, not any walking.
`internal/reflectlite.Swapper` alone is 15.72% of all allocations in the
after tree.

### CPU agrees

    $ go tool pprof -top -cum   (after tree, 50 iterations)
      1.18s 51.98%  cmd.structFields
      1.05s 46.26%  cmd.typeFields
      0.39s 17.18%  cmd.isBlock
      0.38s 16.74%  runtime.mallocgc
      0.27s 11.89%  runtime.gcBgMarkWorker

vs the before tree, where `structFields` cum is 41.73% and `jsonName`
24.46%.

### Mechanism, stated once

`typeFields` allocates a fixed ~11-object scaffold (two reflect-based
sorts, two maps, one slice) on EVERY call. `renderYAML` calls it once per
struct VALUE, and twice for a struct that is a mapping value — 3 calls
per corpus entry, a shape that is unchanged from before d7w5.11. The
regression is (new fixed per-resolution cost) x (pre-existing
per-value call count). Neither factor alone is the cause; the port made
one resolution ~1.7x more expensive and the renderer was already buying
7,303 of them.

comments.author: coordinator-d7w5
comments.text:
## Pass 3 of 5 — SCALING. Linear in corpus size; the distinct-type set is
## fixed at 3 and never grows.

### Resolutions are exactly 3n+1

Counter probe, same instrumented build, varying corpus size:

    n=1      typeFields calls=4      distinct types=3
    n=10     typeFields calls=31     distinct types=3
    n=100    typeFields calls=301    distinct types=3
    n=1000   typeFields calls=3001   distinct types=3
    n=2434   typeFields calls=7303   distinct types=3

3n+1 exactly: one `headingsResult`, n `headingMatch`, 2n `Span`. The
distinct-type count is a property of the RESULT TYPE and is 3 whatever
the corpus does.

### Cost per entry is constant, so total cost is linear

    $ go test ./cmd -run '^$' -bench BenchmarkYztvScale -benchtime 30x -benchmem

    n       before ns/op   after ns/op   memo ns/op | before a/e  after a/e  memo a/e
    100        891,608     1,524,133      579,993  |   52.93      85.98      18.92
    609      5,316,240     9,449,719    3,424,545  |   54.35      87.36      20.34
    1000     9,683,195    16,187,646    5,940,054  |   54.51      87.52      20.50
    2434    23,086,110    38,079,950   14,671,914  |   54.65      87.66      20.65
    5000    44,943,354    78,504,840   29,578,737  |   54.65      87.65      20.64

(a/e = allocs per corpus entry.) Flat at every size. The after-minus-
before delta is **33.0 allocs per entry**, constant — 11 per resolution
x 3 resolutions per entry.

### The answer

The cost is **per VALUE, linear in corpus size**, not per distinct type.
This is not "linear in a small fixed set of types": the set of distinct
types is 3 and fixed, and those 3 answers are recomputed 7,303 times at
n=2,434 and 15,001 times at n=5,000. The INFORMATION computed is O(1) in
the corpus; the WORK is O(corpus).

### What the real command actually renders

The bead's 2,434 does not reproduce. Measured on this repository today,
with binaries built from both scratch trees and run from the repo root:

    $ spec headings | grep -c '  - path:'
    before: 609        after: 609
    $ spec index --out - | (count headings arrays)
    total headings in index: 609

`spec headings` with no operand selects every heading in the corpus and
returns **609** matches, not 2,434 — so the real workload is ~1,828
resolutions, and the true figure is 4x smaller than the bead records.
`--emit` and `--json` are the only other flags; there is no broader
selection.

End-to-end wall time of the whole command on the real corpus, median of
7 warm runs each:

    before  97.1 ms      after 102.2 ms      memo 95.5 ms

The YAML rendering at n=609 is 5.3 ms before / 9.4 ms after in isolation,
and the 4.1 ms isolated delta matches the ~5 ms end-to-end delta. So on
the corpus as it stands the regression costs ~4-5 ms of a ~100 ms
command, not 39.8 ms of a 50 ms budget. The AC-SPEC-009.1 framing on the
bead rests on the 2,434 figure and should be re-derived from 609.

`renderYAML` has exactly one non-test caller in the tree —
`headings.go:243` — so `spec headings` is the whole blast radius.

comments.author: coordinator-d7w5
comments.text:
## Pass 4 of 5 — the pre-change baseline was ALSO doing avoidable work.
## Recorded as a finding; no remedy is proposed or implied.

The bead's `sync.Map` prototype beating the pre-change code is not an
artifact. It holds, and the reason is checkable.

### It holds

Prototype reproduced from scratch (package-level `sync.Map`,
load-or-store around the existing resolver, `uncachedTypeFields`
otherwise untouched). Same bytes out — sha256 `1088869c...`, identical to
both other trees — and `go test ./cmd` fully green.

    n=2434     ns/op        allocs/op
    before   23,086,110      133,024
    after    38,079,950      213,371
    memo     14,671,914       50,258

Memoized is **1.57x faster than the PRE-change code** and uses **2.65x
fewer allocations** (20.65/entry vs 54.65).

### Why: the old code re-parsed every json tag, per field, per value

Alloc profile of the pre-change tree, `alloc_objects`, 6,001,750 total:

    ROUTINE cmd.jsonName    2162786 flat / 4030589 cum = 67.16% of Total
       .    1867803   L359:  parts := strings.Split(tag, ",")
    2162786 2162786   L363:  opts := map[string]bool{}

**Two thirds of every allocation the pre-change renderer made was
re-parsing json struct tags** — a `strings.Split` and a
`map[string]bool` per field per value, for a tag string that is a
compile-time constant. `strings.genSplit` alone is 31.12% of all
allocations.

Both versions therefore recompute a per-TYPE answer per VALUE. d7w5.11
made each recomputation ~1.7x dearer; it did not introduce the
recomputation.

### What this means for the word "restore"

"Restoring" the pre-d7w5.11 performance would mean returning to a
baseline that was itself ~2.6x above the achievable floor for identical
output. The 1.81x regression and the pre-existing ~2.6x headroom are two
separate facts, and the second one was never a d7w5.11 side effect.

Stating it because it bears on what the target would be; the choice of
target, and whether to change anything at all, is not mine and I make no
recommendation. Two things a decision would want that I did not
investigate, both firmly remedy-side: whether any value reachable through
`renderYAML` could make a per-type cache unbounded or recursive, and
whether cache residency across goroutines matters for a single-shot CLI.

comments.author: coordinator-d7w5
comments.text:
## Pass 5 of 5 — WHAT I COULD NOT ESTABLISH

1. **Where 2,434 came from.** The bead calls it "the size of this
   repository's own corpus, i.e. spec headings with no selection". I
   measure 609, from both the before and the after binary, and the index
   itself carries 609 headings. I could not find any invocation of `spec
   headings` that yields 2,434 — the command has only `--emit` and
   `--json`, neither of which widens the selection. **Settled by:** the
   exact invocation, `specs.toml` roots and commit the retro measured
   under. Until then the ratios on this bead stand and the absolute
   millisecond figures — including the AC-SPEC-009.1 comparison — do not.

2. **Whether the 50 ms budget is breached.** Every number here is from a
   4-core Xeon @2.10GHz container with a warm build cache. AC-SPEC-009.1
   names 50 ms but I did not establish what reference environment it is
   measured on, so I cannot say whether ~102 ms end-to-end (or the ~9.4
   ms of it that is YAML rendering) is over or under. **Settled by:** the
   FRD's reference environment, if it names one, plus a run there.

3. **The sub-allocation split of the remaining ~4 of the +11.** I
   measured `visited` + `nextCount` + `next` at 4 allocations together
   and the two sorts at 6 exactly; I did not separate those 4, and 6+4=10
   against a measured 11, so ~1 alloc per resolution is unattributed
   (most likely `fields` slice growth differing between the two shapes).
   **Settled by:** a build with a counter at each allocation site.

4. **Behaviour on types with embedded structs.** Both live types are
   flat, so the BFS loop runs one round and `next` is always empty. The
   claim "the walk itself costs nothing" is established FOR THESE TYPES
   only. A result type with embedding would run more rounds and allocate
   another `nextCount` map per round. **Settled by:** the same probe over
   a type with embedded structs — the shipped 16-case differential suite
   has such types.

5. **Whether any of this is user-visible.** ~5 ms on a ~100 ms command,
   measured as wall time from a warm shell. No latency requirement was
   checked against a real user path. **Settled by:** whatever consumes
   `spec headings` output and cares.

### Method notes

Everything ran in `git archive` copies under the session scratchpad; five
trees (before / after / probe-instrumented / memo prototype / no-sort
diagnostic), none inside the repository. Confirmed after the last
measurement: `git status --porcelain --untracked-files=all -- cli/` is
empty, and nothing in the working tree is mine. Two `docs/retros` edits
and two `.sf/outbox` files appeared in `git status` mid-investigation and
belong to a concurrent session (commit 892b9b7, timestamps 23:12-23:15);
`git diff --stat 62e9e42..892b9b7 -- cli/` is empty, so that work does
not touch the code under study.

title: Decide whether Identifier should collapse hyphen runs and trim leading/trailing hyphens
description:
## Problem

markdown.Identifier's documented derivation removes every character that
is not a letter, digit, hyphen, underscore or space and maps each
remaining space to a hyphen. It does not collapse a run of hyphens and
does not trim one, so removed punctuation sitting beside a space leaves
both hyphens.

Measured on the run branch after agent-plugins-d7w5.8, with
go build -C cli -o spec ./spec:

  spec headings specs/standards/work-order-definition-of-ready.md --json
    "3. `## Design` present (non-trivial, non-epic orders)"
        -> 3--design-present-non-trivial-non-epic-orders
    "7. Tier assigned (+ reason)"      -> 7-tier-assigned--reason
    "4. `## Acceptance` criteria ..."  -> 4--acceptance-criteria-kind-bug--kind-feature

  and in package markdown:
    Identifier("## Not a heading here") -> "-not-a-heading-here"
    Identifier("> quoted")              -> "-quoted"

This predates d7w5.8 for the punctuation cases — the existing, committed
test case already documents it:
cli/core/markdown/headings_test.go asserts
Identifier("Corpus in [[module-document-core]] (modified) — IDX") ==
"corpus-in-module-document-core-modified--idx", a double hyphen from the
dropped em dash. d7w5.8 only added the leading-hyphen cases, by making a
block-level marker a literal character of the heading's name.

## Why it is a question and not a bug

agent-plugins-d7w5.8's problem statement cites the anchor convention "a
reader would guess", naming GitHub. Whether GitHub itself collapses these
runs is UNVERIFIED here — no network probe of a rendered GitHub anchor was
run in this container, and reasoning about its algorithm is not evidence.
What would settle it: publish a document containing the headings above to
a GitHub-rendered README and read the anchor ids out of the rendered HTML,
or find the anchor generator's own test corpus.

Two answers, and this bead is to pick one:

1. Leave it. The derivation is simple, documented in the Markdown
   Structure component block of
   specs/modules/document-core/document-core-module.md, pure, and already
   asserted by tests.
2. Collapse runs and trim ends. Closer to a reader's guess, but it changes
   the documented derivation, breaks the committed "modified--idx"
   assertion, and silently changes the identifier of every corpus heading
   whose text carries punctuation beside a space — the identifier is the
   whole key of the <document>#<heading> addressing grammar, so that is a
   corpus-wide change of meaning, not a cosmetic one.

Out of scope for d7w5.8, whose Design says only rendered() changes and
whose chosen fix leaves the character filter exactly as it is.

title: cli-output-standards' conformance table and status line are hand-maintained, unchecked, and false again
description:
`specs/standards/cli-output-standards.md` carries two hand-maintained claims
about the whole command surface — a status line and the preamble to its "Current
conformance" table — and nothing checks either. Both were false from the day the
document was written, because the document itself says the first conforming
command will falsify them. Run `agent-plugins-d7w5` falsified them again by
landing `headings`, and the only thing that caught it was an agent noticing
mid-bead.

THE FINDING THAT RAISED IT (`f6tl.4#4`, run `agent-plugins-d7w5`; record:
docs/retros/2026-09-04-d7w5-spec-corpus-structure-extraction.md):

> retro:scope Landing this item made cli-output-standards' own status text
> false, so the standards document had to change with it — the item's c4_docs
> names only spec-cli-container.md.
> evidence: The document read 'Status: approved, and not yet met' and its
> conformance table 'No command conforms today; the surface predates these
> standards.' Both become untrue the moment a conforming command exists, and the
> same document says 'A command specified after this document is written to
> conform from the start' — so the falsehood was built into it from the day it
> was written.

MEASURED 2026-09-04, AFTER that repair, and the preamble is FALSE AGAIN. The
table's preamble now reads:

> Every command below predates these standards and none of them conforms yet;
> `headings`, specified after them, conforms and is listed last.

while two rows of the table it introduces say otherwise:

> | `links <path>` | the rewritten document | conforms — a document payload,
>   written as itself |
> | `headings <selection>` | ... | conforms — written against these standards ...

`links` predates the standards and conforms, so "every command below predates
these standards and none of them conforms yet" is untrue of the table directly
beneath it. That is the second falsification in one document in one run, which
is the evidence that the defect is the hand-maintained universal claim rather
than any particular sentence.

WHAT IT COSTS. A standards document that asserts something the tree contradicts
is worse than one that asserts nothing: an agent reading "no command conforms
today" concludes the standards are aspirational and writes a non-conforming
command. The cost also lands on grooming — the dependency is invisible from a
bead's own C4 blast radius, so a bead adding a conforming command does not know
it must edit this document, which is what `agent-plugins-d7w5.15` filed and what
the general grooming rule tracks separately.

ANCHORS.
- `specs/standards/cli-output-standards.md` — the paragraph beginning
  "**Status: approved, and met by the commands specified since.**", and the
  section headed "## Current conformance" with its preamble beginning
  "Measured with a binary built from this branch" and its `| command | prints
  today | to conform |` table.
- `cli/cmd/registry.go` and the command files beside it — where a command is
  registered, and therefore where a new row's obligation is created.
- `swarm.toml` `[[checks]]` — where a new check id is declared; `scripts/ci.sh`
  runs the contributor list.
- Measured command set today, `build/spec --help`: check, criterion, feature,
  headings, index, links, next-id, refs, slug-exists (9, excluding `help`),
  against 8 table rows because `feature` and `criterion` share one.
design:
Delete the universal claims, keep the per-command rows, and add a check that
enforces the one thing about the table that IS mechanizable: that every command
the CLI registers has a row, and no row names a command that does not exist.

The choice this bead settles, so it is not re-litigated: the conformance table is
NOT derived. Deriving it would mean deciding, in code, whether each command's
output conforms to a prose standard — that is the judgement the standard exists
to record, and a generator asserting it would be asserting something nobody
measured. What IS derivable is the row set, and that is the drift the document
actually suffers: a command lands, the document is not touched, and it silently
describes a smaller surface than exists.

DOCUMENT CHANGES, in `specs/standards/cli-output-standards.md`.

1. The status paragraph loses its corpus-wide verdict. "Status: approved, and met
   by the commands specified since" is a claim over every command; replace it
   with a pointer to the table — the status of the document is `approved`, which
   its frontmatter already carries, and per-command conformance is the table's
   business and nowhere else's.

2. The table preamble loses "Every command below predates these standards and
   none of them conforms yet". Keep the sentence that says how the table was
   measured (the binary, the corpus), because that is provenance and stays true.

3. Every conformance statement lives in a row's own "to conform" cell, which is
   already the case. Nothing outside the table says how many commands conform, so
   nothing outside the table can be falsified by adding one.

THE CHECK. A new script, following the shape of the existing corpus checks
(`scripts/check-reference-links.py`, `scripts/check-template-drift.py` — python3,
repository-root-relative, exit 0 or 1 with a per-failure line). It:

- builds or locates the `spec` binary and reads the command set from
  `spec --help`'s "Available Commands", discarding `help`;
- parses the `| command | prints today | to conform |` table out of
  `specs/standards/cli-output-standards.md`, taking each row's first cell and
  splitting it on `,` so a shared row such as `` `feature`, `criterion` `` yields
  both names; strips backticks and any operand suffix (`<slug>`, `[path]`,
  `<selection>`);
- fails when the two sets differ, naming each missing and each extra command.

Declare it in `swarm.toml` as a new `[[checks]]` entry (suggested id
`cli-conformance-table`) so it runs per bead, and it is picked up by
`scripts/ci.sh` through the same list. It is fast — one already-built binary
invocation and one file read — which is the test for belonging in the per-bead
list rather than in CI alone.

Rejected: a check that greps the document for universal quantifiers ("no
command", "every command"). It cannot tell a claim about the command surface from
a rule about it — this document is full of legitimate universals such as "They
apply to every subcommand, present and future" — so it would either fire on the
rules or miss the claims.
acceptance_criteria:
- [ ] `specs/standards/cli-output-standards.md` contains no assertion about how many commands conform; the status paragraph and the "Current conformance" preamble each carry no corpus-wide verdict
- [ ] The preamble sentence "Every command below predates these standards and none of them conforms yet" is gone, and no replacement sentence states a fact the table's own rows can contradict
- [ ] Per-command conformance is stated only in the table's rows, and `links` and `headings` still read as conforming
- [ ] The provenance sentence saying the table was measured with a binary built from this branch, run against this repository's corpus, is retained
- [ ] A new check script exists, exits 0 on the current tree, and exits 1 with a naming message when a command is registered without a table row, and again when a row names a command the CLI does not register
- [ ] The check derives the command set from the built `spec` binary's own command list rather than from a second hand-maintained list
- [ ] The check handles a row naming more than one command, so the shared `feature`, `criterion` row satisfies both
- [ ] The check is declared in `swarm.toml` as a `[[checks]]` entry with an `id` and a `command`, and running `scripts/ci.sh` exercises it
- [ ] `cd cli && go build ./...` and `cd cli && go test ./...` both exit 0
- [ ] `build/spec check --strict` exits 0

metadata.tier_reason: Removes claims from a normative standards document without weakening it, and adds a new declared check whose parser must tolerate the tables shared and operand-suffixed rows; a wrong check either fires on the documents legitimate universals or never fires at all.

title: Bead f6tl.4 edited cli-output-standards.md without declaring it in c4_docs, so the collision graph could not have serialized it
description:
REVIEW FINDING (run agent-plugins-d7w5, pass 1). CLASSIFIED OUT OF SCOPE — see the verdict at the end. This is a grooming-accuracy finding, not a code defect.

MEASURED. `bd show agent-plugins-f6tl.4 --json` metadata:

    "c4_docs": ["specs/containers/spec-cli/spec-cli-container.md"]

`git diff 70dddef..HEAD --stat` shows the commit for that bead (ef94bd1) also changed:

    specs/standards/cli-output-standards.md | 16 +-

THE EDIT ITSELF IS CORRECT AND WAS NECESSARY. That standard carried two claims the new `headings` command falsified the moment it landed:

    -**Status: approved, and not yet met.**
    -... No command conforms today; the surface predates these standards.

Leaving them would have shipped a standards document asserting something the same commit made false. The batch agent changed them and added a `headings` row to the conformance table. Right call.

THE FINDING IS THE UNDER-DECLARATION. `c4_docs` is what swarm-plan reads to compute co-edit collision edges and serialize beads that touch the same document. A bead that edits a document it did not declare is invisible to that computation: had a sibling bead in this run also touched cli-output-standards.md, the two would have been dispatched concurrently onto the same file with nothing serializing them. No harm here — no sibling touched it — but the graph was wrong, not merely lucky.

THE GENERALIZABLE POINT, which is why this is worth a bead rather than a shrug: a document that records "no command conforms today" is falsified by ANY bead that adds a conforming command. That dependency is not visible from the bead's own C4 blast radius, because the standard is not a C4 element the command changes — it is a document making a universal claim over the surface. Grooming has no step that asks "which documents assert something this change makes false?"

VERDICT — OUT OF SCOPE for this run. Row 3. Nothing in the merged diff is wrong; the artifact at fault is a bead's metadata, and the bead is closed. The value is in the retro, for grooming and for swarm-plan's collision model.

SUGGESTED REMEDY, for whoever takes it: add a grooming prompt — when a bead adds the first conforming instance of a standard, the standard's own document belongs in c4_docs — and consider whether a check can spot a standards document containing a universal claim ("no command", "every command") that a diff in the same commit contradicts.

title: RecordBlock.content is [String: String], which cannot carry a nested value a stage-2 tag may register
description:
REVIEW FINDING (run agent-plugins-d7w5, pass 1). CLASSIFIED OUT OF SCOPE for this run — see the verdict at the end.

WHERE: schemas/index.strata, struct `RecordBlock`:

    """
    The block's content, parsed in the format its tag declares.

    A mapping of property name to value as written. Strata models closed
    shapes, so an open record is a map rather than an arbitrary value, and
    this framework's element declarations — a title, a description and a
    slug — are exactly that shape. ...
    """
    content: [String: String]

WHAT: the type admits only a flat string-to-string mapping. A record-block tag registering a format with nested values — JSON or TOML with a nested table, or YAML with a sequence or sub-mapping — has no representation. The comment justifies the choice by the shapes THIS framework declares today (title, description, slug), which is true of those three and is not a property of the format.

STATE TODAY, measured: nothing populates it. `grep -rn "RecordBlocks" cli/core --include=*.go | grep -v _test` shows `corpus.go` assigning `[]specmodel.RecordBlock{}` and nothing else; every heading and entry carries an empty list. The property is inert in stage 1.

WHY IT IS WORTH A BEAD ANYWAY: `content` ships now as a property of a schema carrying a `schema_version`, in the generated JSON Schema, the generated Go model, the generated markdown reference and the committed manifest.json fixtures. Widening `[String: String]` later is a breaking change to a published shape; deciding it now, before anything consumes it, is nearly free.

VERDICT — OUT OF SCOPE. Row 3 of the review criteria. It is not a defect of stage 1: nothing populates `content`, so no behaviour is wrong today, and the remedy is a design decision belonging to the record-block tag registration FEAT-SPECSTR-004 specifies — which the authorization gate excluded from this run (agent-plugins-f6tl.5, .6, .7 deferred). A finding that amounts to "stage 2 is not done" is out of scope by construction.

FOR WHOEVER TAKES STAGE 2: settle the type before a consumer exists. If the answer is that a record block is only ever flat, say so in the Strata doc comment as a CONSTRAINT ON THE TAG REGISTRATION rather than as an observation about three current declarations, so the next reader does not have to re-derive it.

title: markdown.Headings is unsafe on a whole file with frontmatter, and a negative-control test pins the misbehaviour
description:
REVIEW FINDING (run agent-plugins-d7w5, pass 1). Row 1: cli/core/markdown/headings.go and its test are new in this run.

WHAT: `markdown.Headings(src)` over a whole file reports the entire YAML frontmatter block as a level-2 SETEXT heading, because the blocks closing `---` underlines the YAML above it and CommonMark reads that as a setext underline. The package documents frontmatter separation as a caller concern, and `corpus.headingsOf` is the only caller that honours it — by passing a body offset.

MEASURED, from the runs own test cli/core/markdown/headings_test.go (TestASearchFromTheBodyOffsetLeavesTheFrontmatterBehind), src = "---\ntitle: Example\nslug: adr-001\n---\n\n# Real\n\nbody\n":

    markdown.Headings(src) -> 2 headings; whole[0].Level == 2
                              whole[0].Text == "title: Example\nslug: adr-001"

THE TEST LOCK IS THE ACTIONABLE PART. That tests negative control ASSERTS the misbehaviour:

    whole := markdown.Headings(src)
    if len(whole) != 2 || whole[0].Level != 2 {
        t.Fatalf("expected the whole-file search to report the frontmatter as a level-2 heading, got %+v", whole)
    }
    if whole[0].Text != "title: Example\nslug: adr-001" {
        t.Errorf("the control did not reproduce the frontmatter-as-heading case: %q", whole[0].Text)
    }

So the suite FAILS if the package is ever taught to handle frontmatter correctly. A test that fails on a fix is a trap for a future agent, who will read a red suite as a regression rather than as a stale control.

WHY IT MATTERS: `Headings` is exported and its only safety property lives in a doc comment. This is the same underlying hazard that bites in production through the corpus fallback path (see the sibling finding on `headingsOf`s closing delimiter); this bead is the API and test side of it.

FIX, either: (a) teach the package to skip a leading frontmatter block itself and delete the control; or (b) keep the caller-concern contract but re-express the control so it asserts the CONTRACT ("a whole-file search is not frontmatter-aware") rather than the exact wrong output, and say in the test comment that a fix at this layer means deleting it, not repairing it.

title: A heading with no text is skipped entirely, so it never closes the section above it
description:
REVIEW FINDING (run agent-plugins-d7w5, pass 1). Row 1: cli/core/markdown/headings.go is new in this run.

WHERE: cli/core/markdown/headings.go — the walk skips a heading node with no text segment rather than recording it (the guard sits immediately before the heading is appended).

WHAT: a bare `##` on a line is a valid CommonMark heading with empty content. The walk drops it, so it is neither reported NOR used to terminate the preceding section.

MEASURED (probe in package markdown_test, runs merged tree), src = "# Real\ntext\n\n##\n\nmore\n":

    h0 level=1 text="Real" section="text\n\n##\n\nmore\n"

One heading, and its section absorbs the empty heading and everything after it.

WHY IT MATTERS: `spec headings doc#real --emit` then emits content belonging to a DIFFERENT section, with no signal that it did. Section spans are the features deliverable; a heading that does not close the section above it makes the span wrong rather than merely incomplete.

The two behaviours are separable and only one is right: the heading has no text to record and arguably should not be a match, but it still has a LINE and a LEVEL and must still close the section above it.

FIX: record the heading for span purposes (so it terminates the preceding section) even when its text is empty; decide separately whether a textless heading is ever a match. If it is excluded from matches, exclude it at the match filter, not at the walk.

title: swarm ready now refuses --threshold 0 but the three surfaces that resolve dispatch_failure_threshold never state the minimum
description:
`agent-plugins-u9uh` made `swarm ready --threshold <n>` refuse any `n < 1`
(search `cli/swarm/cli/ready.go` for the string `so it must be 1 or greater`).
The refusal is right. What it does not do is reach the three surfaces that
decide what value gets passed, none of which states a minimum:

- `sf.toml`, the `[run]` block: "The circuit breaker's threshold: how many
  consecutive dispatch returns that completed no bead stop the RUN. 3 is the
  skill default." (search for `dispatch_failure_threshold`)
- `plugin/skills/sprint-scope/SKILL.md`, the gate table row: "**Circuit-breaker
  threshold** ... | `dispatch_failure_threshold` | 3" (search for
  `Circuit-breaker threshold`)
- `plugin/skills/bead-bonanza/references/dispatching.md`: "**an authorization
  row** (`sf.toml`'s `[run] dispatch_failure_threshold`, else 3)" (search for
  `dispatch_failure_threshold`)

`sf.toml` in the SAME `[run]` block documents `review_budget` as "0 disables
the loop", so "0 turns this off" is an established idiom on that surface. A
project that sets `dispatch_failure_threshold = 0` meaning "no circuit
breaker" now gets: `sprint-scope` resolving 0 into the gate and writing it to
the manifest's `standing_auth`; the human confirming it at the run's single
authorization touchpoint; and then EVERY `swarm ready --run <epic> --threshold
0` in the run exiting with the arguments refusal. The failure lands at each
dispatch return, mid-run, after the one human touchpoint has passed — not at
scope time when it could still be corrected.

Nothing else validates it: `--threshold` is documented in
`specs/architecture/container-swarm-cli.md` as "a flag, not a manifest key",
and `swarm manifest validate` therefore has no rule for
`standing_auth.dispatch_failure_threshold`.

REMEDY (either, or both): state the minimum on the three surfaces above; and/or
reject a non-positive `dispatch_failure_threshold` in `sprint-scope`'s
resolution, so a malformed project default is caught before the gate rather
than at the first dispatch return. If "0 disables the breaker" is the wanted
semantic, that is a third option and it belongs in `ready.go` rather than in
prose.

Introduced by 36598cd (agent-plugins-u9uh): the value was accepted before this
run and is fatal after it. Review finding from run agent-plugins-bguq. IN
SCOPE (row 1), filed not worked (admit_review_findings=false).
close_reason: documentation corrected in 2cf9034; duplicated default recorded and tracked as agent-plugins-jwa8

comments.author: Claude
comments.text:
retro:decision — the coordinator investigated whether `--threshold` is redundant with sf.toml's dispatch_failure_threshold. It is NOT, and this bead should NOT widen into removing the flag.

MEASURED: the swarm CLI does not read sf.toml at all. `grep -rn 'sf\.toml' cli/ --include=*.go` returns exactly one line — swarmmodel.go:100, `AuthSourceProject AuthSource = "sf.toml"` — a string constant used to RECORD where an authorization came from, never to read one.

THE VALUE'S ACTUAL PATH:
  sf.toml [run] dispatch_failure_threshold
    -> resolved by sprint-scope (SKILL.md:220)
    -> recorded in the manifest's standing_auth with its source
    -> passed by the coordinator as `swarm ready --threshold <n>` (dispatching.md:192)
So the flag is the TRANSPORT from skill-resolved config into a deliberately config-agnostic CLI. Removing it would force the Go binary to parse the skill's TOML, which is the coupling the split exists to avoid.

WHAT IS ACTUALLY WRONG, and it is worse than the doc drift this bead already names: THE DEFAULT IS DUPLICATED. `breakerDefaultThreshold = 3` at ready.go:309 and "3" in sprint-scope's table are two independent literals for one authorized value. If they ever diverge, a run that omits --threshold silently runs at a threshold DIFFERENT from the one standing_auth records as authorized — and the manifest would still read as though the human had approved the value actually in force.

So this bead stands as filed (a documentation defect: three documents describe the flag as merely defaulting to 3, while u9uh made <1 fatal and the same sf.toml block uses 0-means-off for review_budget), PLUS the duplicated literal above. The remedy is documentation and de-duplication, not removing the flag.

comments.author: coordinator-bguq
comments.text:
retro:decision — fixed as documentation, in commit 2cf9034. The flag is NOT removed.

title: recheckDispatchBeads' new guard is justified by a false claim, and its refusal discards the fold's facts after an irreversible merge
description:
`cli/swarm/cli/accept_settle.go`, in `recheckDispatchBeads`, replaced
`beadsInv := invocationsOf(recs)` with a guard that can return an error, and
justified it with this comment (search the file for the string
`so none of them rescues an empty beadsInv`):

    // The three other contributors to inv below are each appended under a
    // nil guard, so none of them rescues an empty beadsInv.
    beadsInv, err := invocationsRequired("the beads under "+req.Run, recs)

The inference is invalid. Further down the same function (search for
`inv := [][]string{}`) the assembly is:

    inv := [][]string{}
    inv = append(inv, beadsInv...)
    if commitInv != nil { inv = append(inv, commitInv) }
    if wtInv != nil { inv = append(inv, wtInv) }
    if ancestorInv != nil { inv = append(inv, ancestorInv) }

The nil guards mean those three are appended WHEN NON-NIL. Any one of them
being non-nil makes `inv` non-empty, which is exactly "rescuing an empty
beadsInv". What the comment presumably means — that they cannot be RELIED on,
since all three may be nil — is a different and much weaker claim, and it is
not what the sentence says. `beads_checked` and `acceptance_failures` are the
only facts built from `inv`, and neither could reach `Result.Validate`'s
"names no invocation" rule from an empty `beadsInv` alone.

WHY IT MATTERS BEYOND THE PROSE. `invocationsRequired` returns
`RefuseUnrepairable(...)`, a plain `*Refusal` and not an `*acceptStop`.
`recheckDispatchBeads` is called from `settleDispatch`, which is called from
`acceptDispatch` AFTER `foldIn` has already run `git merge --ff-only` — an
irreversible write. `acceptDispatch` answers a non-`acceptStop` error from
`settleDispatch` with `return Result{}, err` (search accept.go for
`settled, recs, err := settleDispatch`), so every fact established so far —
including `merged: true` and `merged_sha` — is discarded and the caller gets a
bare refusal that cannot tell it the fold already happened. That is precisely
the loss agent-plugins-4ca8 and agent-plugins-j5ah were filed to prevent, and
this change adds one more way to reach it.

The severity is bounded, not zero: the run's own test-file header
(cli/swarm/cli/citation_test.go, the block beginning "Why sites 1, 2 and 3 are
covered at their guard and not end to end") records three measured guards that
make this error path unreachable today — `tracker.Descendants` cannot answer
successfully with records nothing cites. So this is a latent defect behind a
false rationale, not a live one. The rationale is the part a future reader
will act on.

REMEDY: correct the comment to say what is true (the three contributors may
all be nil, so none can be RELIED on), and — separately — make the post-fold
half of `acceptDispatch` carry its established facts onto a plain refusal the
way `acceptStopped` already does for an `*acceptStop`.

Introduced by 82d575f (agent-plugins-f9lq). Review finding from run
agent-plugins-bguq. IN SCOPE (row 1), filed not worked
(admit_review_findings=false).

comments.author: coordinator-bguq
comments.text: retro: The comment was false as filed, and correcting it needed a THIRD reading rather than the weaker one the bead proposed. The bead suggested "the three contributors may all be nil, so none can be relied on". That is a reachability claim I did not measure — invocationOf (wtInv) always answers from the step declaration, and commitInv/ancestorInv come from argvOf on records their producers already refused when they did not run — so I would have replaced one unmeasured universal with another. The comment now states only what is structurally true and needs no measurement: the beads read is what establishes beads_checked and the per-bead half of acceptance_failures, and the other three cite reads that establish nothing about which beads the dispatch holds, so an inv made non-empty by one of them would carry a citation a reader could re-run and still not reproduce the answer. That is why the guard is on beadsInv early and not on inv at assembly.

comments.author: coordinator-bguq
comments.text: retro: The guard condition is merged.ran and not the error kind, which is what keeps the pre-fold behaviour identical. TestASettleHalfRefusalBeforeAnyFoldStillAbandonsTheAccept is the negative control for that boundary: a dry run refuses the fast-forward, still reaches the ancestry read (a read), and its failure is still answered with a bare refusal carrying no merged fact — so "degrade instead of abandoning" was not widened to a path with nothing to preserve. The second control, TestASettleHalfThatAnswersStillAcceptsCleanly, runs the same world with the ancestry read answering and gets a clean accept with an established merged_sha.

comments.author: coordinator-bguq
comments.text: retro: The fact loss is LIVE, not latent — the bead scoped the severity to the uncited-beads guard, which citation_test.go shows is unreachable, but the same return statement is reached by every plain refusal the settle half raises, and readAncestry raises one on any ancestry read that fails outright. Measured: with the fold succeeding (git merge --ff-only, then the post-fold resolve answering 2222...) and git merge-base --is-ancestor bb/dev-1 sprint/run-1 exiting 128, the pre-fix command printed outcome stop with "facts": [] — merged and merged_sha both gone after a fast-forward that cannot be undone. Exit 128 rather than 1 is what makes it a failure instead of an answer, since git.Descends declares Answers = []int{1}. So the test drives the mechanism end to end through a reachable entrance rather than at the one entrance that is currently only a defence.

comments.author: coordinator-bguq
comments.text: retro: acceptDegraded deliberately does NOT reuse acceptStopped, and the difference is the resolution. acceptStopped SUBSTITUTES the refusal resolution for whatever the result carried; a settle-half refusal after a fold that already reported an unestablished merged_sha would then drop the resolution describing a write that happened. acceptDegraded appends instead — the same composition settleDispatch already uses for its own attention verdict, and the property TestBothHalvesNeedingAttentionKeepBothResolutions pins on the non-error path. A plain settle-half refusal is RefuseUnrepairable and carries no resolution of its own, so one is named there: the fold is not undone, so settling the named condition and accepting the dispatch again is the remedy. Worth noting acceptStopped has the same substitution defect on its own path (the not-an-ancestor acceptStop discards a merged_sha resolution); left alone as out of this bead scope, and filable if it matters.
