title: Split subagent-prompts.md into one prompt file per worker
description:
## Decision

Owner's call in PR #27 review (discussion_r3839727221): "I think we should
break this file up into one `-prompt` file per worker the orchestrator spawns."

## Today

`plugin/skills/bead-bonanza/references/subagent-prompts.md` is 24,641 bytes and
carries five distinct things:

| section | what it is |
|---|---|
| Per-bead subagent prompt template | a prompt |
| Shared batch preamble | a prompt fragment, included by the next two |
| Doc/chore fast-lane subagent prompt template | a prompt |
| Shared-surface batch subagent prompt template | a prompt |
| Worktree mechanics (orchestrator) | NOT a prompt — the base-ref trap, bd inside a worktree, the create/merge/remove lifecycle, concurrent dispatch |

An orchestrator dispatching one fast-lane batch loads all of it.

## Wanted

One file per worker it spawns, plus a home for the part that is not a prompt:

    references/prompt-per-bead.md
    references/prompt-fast-lane.md
    references/prompt-shared-surface.md
    references/worktree-mechanics.md

The "shared batch preamble" is included by two of the three, so it either gets
its own file both cite, or it is duplicated into both. Duplication is defensible
here — each prompt file should be readable and pasteable on its own — but it
must then be generated rather than hand-maintained, or the two copies drift.

## Constraint

`check-reference-links.py` fails a backticked path that does not resolve from
the file, so each new file must be self-contained. The reference table in
`bead-bonanza/SKILL.md` needs a row per file, and the coordinator's body is at
the ~20,000-byte cap — see `agent-plugins-ia3y.5`, which may need to land first.
design:
Split `plugin/skills/bead-bonanza/references/subagent-prompts.md`
(24,641 bytes, five sections) into four files:

  references/prompt-per-bead.md        the per-bead subagent template
  references/prompt-fast-lane.md       the doc/chore fast-lane template
  references/prompt-shared-surface.md  the shared-surface batch template
  references/worktree-mechanics.md     NOT a prompt: the base-ref trap, bd
                                       inside a worktree, the create/merge/
                                       remove lifecycle, concurrent dispatch

THE SHARED PREAMBLE is the wrinkle. Two of the three prompt files include it.
Each prompt file must be readable and pasteable alone, so duplicate it rather
than cross-referencing - but then it MUST be generated, or the copies drift.
Extend `scripts/sync-shared-references.sh` (which already vendors generated
copies and has a `--check` mode) to own it, rather than inventing a second
mechanism.

CONSTRAINT: `scripts/check-reference-links.py` fails any backticked path that
does not resolve from the file it appears in, because a skill travels to a
repository with no corpus. Each new file must be self-contained.

`bead-bonanza/SKILL.md`'s reference table needs a row per new file. That body is
at the ~20,000-byte cap, which is why this is blocked on ia3y.5.

NOTE the collision: bead-bonanza/SKILL.md is also edited by b9a0.1, b9a0.2 and
b9a0.3.
acceptance_criteria:
- [ ] One file per dispatchable worker, each readable and pasteable alone.
- [ ] Worktree mechanics is its own file, not mixed with prompt templates.
- [ ] The duplicated preamble is generated and `--check` fails when a copy
      drifts.
- [ ] `bead-bonanza/SKILL.md`'s reference table names every new file.
- [ ] `scripts/check-reference-links.py` reports 0 errors.
- [ ] scripts/ci.sh exits 0.
close_reason: Split into six files; the duplicated preamble is generated by sync-shared-references.sh with a --check that was proven to bite. ci.sh exits 0.

metadata.tier_reason: a file split is mechanical, but the generated-preamble mechanism and the self-containment constraint are design work

It said `check-reference-links.py` fails a backticked path that does not resolve; that script's docstring says it reads markdown link syntax only (`[text](target)`) and deliberately does NOT parse anything else. The gate that fails a backticked path is scripts/check-skills.sh check 2. Both were run and both pass, so nothing was missed — but a future bead copying this constraint would test the wrong thing.

I also added a block-orphan guard mirroring the existing header-orphan guard, because the same fail-open hazard applies — a marker telling readers not to edit a span that nothing regenerates. Both new guards were proven to bite by sabotage: tampering with a generated copy reports STALE (block) and exits 1; adding a marker with no BLOCKS entry reports ORPHAN and exits 1.

That gives prompt-placeholders.md, prompt-per-bead.md, prompt-fast-lane.md, prompt-shared-surface.md, prompt-batch-preamble.md (the authored source of the duplicated block) and worktree-mechanics.md.

title: bead-bonanza/SKILL.md is structurally at the 20,000-byte cap
description:
## Problem

The body hit the cap three times across two sessions. The one-worktree-per-
dispatch change needed ~180 bytes of new text and cost a dozen unrelated prose
trims to find them — trims to the report section, the review budget, the
circuit breaker, none of which the change touched.

That is a tax on every future edit, paid in edits to text unrelated to the
change being made, which is how unrelated regressions get introduced.

## Scope

Move a section out to a reference rather than keep shaving. Candidates, by
size and by how often the coordinator actually needs them inline:

- "Every dispatch runs in its own worktree" — the lifecycle already lives in
  `references/subagent-prompts.md`; only the hard gate needs to be inline.
- "Review the run's own diff" — the loop is the coordinator's, but the budget
  rationale is reference material.

The run-health table already moved to `references/run-record.md` on this
branch, which is the pattern.

## Acceptance criteria

[ ] The body is under 18,000 bytes, leaving headroom for the next change.
[ ] No rule is lost — each moved section is reachable from the reference table.
[ ] scripts/ci.sh exits 0.

comments.author: Claude
comments.text: retro:proof:skill-body-cap — body measured at 19,993 bytes before and 17,966 after, verified with a byte count over the frontmatter-stripped body rather than the file. Five sections moved to references rather than compressed: supervision (new file), the review-loop budget, base_sha's rationale, the circuit breaker, and why nothing escalates mid-run. check-skills.sh --strict and scripts/ci.sh both exit 0.

title: Report upstream: bd swarm list shows closed molecules as Active
description:
Measured on bd 1.2.2. 'bd swarm list' prints a heading of 'Active Swarms (N)' and includes swarm molecules whose own status is closed.

Reproduction:
  bd swarm create <epic>          # note the molecule id
  bd close <molecule-id>
  bd swarm list                   # still lists it under 'Active Swarms'

Observed: the closed molecule listed with 'Progress: 2/2 (100%)'. Confirmed the molecule's status is 'closed' via bd show --json.

Impact for bead-bonanza: 'swarm list' cannot answer 'which runs are in flight' on its own — every listed molecule's status has to be read separately. agent-plugins-ddvt carries that workaround.

This is an upstream report, not a local fix. Also folds into the standing action to report the other bd defects this review measured.

title: Three check lists disagree: sf.toml, scripts/ci.sh, and the workflows
description:
sf.toml's [[checks]], scripts/ci.sh and .github/workflows/ each carry a different set, with nothing keeping them in step.

- sf.toml (nine): format vet build test-go skills shared-refs strata-docs schemas skills-strict. Read by bead-bonanza, run before every bead's close.
- scripts/ci.sh: go vet, go build, go test, then builds the Spec CLI and runs 'spec index' and 'spec check --strict'. The developer's entry point.
- checks.yml / cli.yml: a fourth arrangement — check-skills.sh (not --strict), sync-shared-references.sh --check, check-reference-links.py, check-template-drift.py, a corpus job running spec check over specs/ and rfcs/, and the Go set across three platforms plus a six-target cross-compile.

Consequences measured this session: a bead editing an ADR runs no corpus validation at all (agent-plugins-1ilc.9 was filed against that gap before ci.sh was found), and a developer running ci.sh runs none of the skills or reference-integrity checks.

Not obviously fixable by collapsing them. The three have different audiences and CI's platform matrix cannot be expressed in a declaration. What has to end is that they diverge silently.

Options: give sf.toml a 'corpus' check invoking the Spec CLI so beads validate specs/; have ci.sh call bb-checks.py for the overlapping subset and keep its spec steps; or accept the split and document in all three places what each deliberately omits and why.
acceptance_criteria: Either the lists share a source for the parts that genuinely overlap, or each of the three states plainly what it omits and why — the current silent divergence is what ends. In particular a bead touching specs/ must have some way to validate the corpus.
close_reason: Closed

title: Stale backticked paths to moved documents in specs/ prose are unenforced by any gate
description:
## Problem

agent-plugins-eaa.2, eaa.3 and eaa.4 moved 14 documents out of
plugin/skills/*/references/ into specs/standards/ and specs/guides/. Prose
inside specs/ still cites several of them by their OLD backticked path.

Known instances, recorded by agent-plugins-eaa.4 while doing the c4-guide move:
c4-guide.md is cited by its pre-move path in ADR-004, ADR-005, ADR-007,
ADR-008, ADR-009, ADR-010, ADR-012, specs/contracts/contract-specs-
configuration.md and specs/standards/blueprint-readiness-checklist.md.
agent-plugins-eaa.2 left an equivalent stale backtick path to
template-authoring-standards.md in ADR-012.

Nothing catches these. scripts/check-skills.sh scans plugin/skills/ only, so it
never reads specs/ prose. spec check --strict validates [[slug]] wikilink forms,
not backticked relative paths. So the citations are wrong and every gate is
green.

This is a gap in coverage, not in any one of the three beads: each declined the
sweep deliberately and consistently, because converting them is unbounded work
with no gate to bound it against.

## Scope note

Filed by the bead-bonanza orchestrator (run 1786686364-15) as OUT-OF-SCOPE
emergent work. No bead in that run fails without it. Not dispatched — awaiting
human triage.

## What a fix would need to decide

Two questions the fix cannot proceed without, and neither is the implementer to
answer:

1. Should a backticked path to a corpus member become a [[wikilink]]? That is
   what eaa.3 and eaa.4 did for the citations they were forced to touch, and it
   is the form spec check can actually validate. Applying it corpus-wide is a
   larger editorial change than either bead made.
2. Should a gate enforce it? A checker for backticked paths that resolve to
   nothing would need to distinguish a citation from an illustrative example --
   the same citation-vs-example judgement agent-plugins-eaa.1 had to make by
   hand, which is why that bead was sized at ~50 edits and turned out to be 3.

Answering (2) yes probably subsumes agent-plugins-bru, which records that
check-skills.sh skips five path prefixes so a dangling docs/ or scripts/
reference in a skill is never caught.

title: Move the 6 shipped guides into specs/guides and vendor them outward
description:
The same treatment as the standards move, for the guide-typed documents the plugin ships.

The 6: guide-c4 (c4-guide.md — but see below), guide-ears, guide-document-type-boundaries, guide-spec-anti-patterns, spec-cli-reference, work-order-field-guide.

specs/guides/ does not exist yet; specs/ currently holds adrs, architecture, contracts, features and standards. This bead creates it.

Lower priority than the standards move and separable from it: the standards are the ones other documents cite, so they carry the citation-resolution benefit. Guides are mostly cited BY skills rather than by other documents.

NOTE: c4-guide is being retyped to a standards document by agent-plugins-wu1. If that lands first, it belongs in the standards move, not here, and this bead covers 5 documents. Check before starting rather than assuming 6.
design:
Follow the standards move exactly — same GENERATED COPY mechanism, same inverted map, same "edit the source" rule.

The one new thing is the directory. specs/guides/ needs to exist and the corpus walk picks it up automatically (the root is specs/, and discovery walks it), so no configuration change is needed.

ears-guide.md deserves a second look while it is being moved, but NOT a retype in this bead: it scores 43 SHALL/MUST in 1479 words, the densest in the repo, which is an artifact of it being a guide ABOUT EARS — most of those are specimens of the pattern (`WHEN [event], the system SHALL [action]`). Two lines are genuinely normative ("Every requirement SHALL use one of the following patterns", "Keywords SHALL be capitalized"). Leaving it a guide is the right call; if the implementer disagrees, file a bead rather than retyping inline.

Same dependency as the standards move: the illustrative-wikilink cleanup lands first.

title: check-template-drift.py: report schema-defined optional properties a template omits
description:
scripts/check-template-drift.py compares a templates frontmatter key set against its types schema definition in two directions but not the third.

Today (lines 155 and 160):
  * `required - keys`  -> template/missing-required
  * `keys - known`     -> template/unknown-property

Missing:
  * `known - keys`     -> an OPTIONAL property the schema defines that the template does not mention

Why it matters: a template is the thing every document of its type is authored from. An optional property absent from the template is a field authors never learn exists — every document silently omits it, and nothing notices. That is a slower, quieter version of the same failure the two existing directions catch.

Not a defect in what the script reports today; a gap in coverage.
design:
Add the third set difference alongside the existing two, at a severity that
reflects what it is: an optional property is optional, so omitting it from a
template is a choice a template author may legitimately make (a rarely-used
field kept out to reduce noise in the scaffold).

That means this SHALL NOT be a hard error like the other two, or the first run
turns green gates red for deliberate omissions.

TAKE OPTION (a): report it as a separate ADVISORY line that does not affect
exit status. The script grows a second severity. This is pinned rather than
left to the implementer because advisory-versus-error changes the script's
exit status, which the CI gate in .github/workflows/checks.yml consumes — an
observable behaviour, not an internal choice.

Rejected, and recorded so it is not re-litigated: option (b), reporting it as
an error with a per-template opt-out comment convention. It is the right shape
only once the inventory shows how many real omissions exist; enforcing before
measuring turns the gate red on deliberate omissions and invites the opt-out to
be used as a mute button. Revisit after (a) has produced the count.

Keep the script dependency-free and YAML-parse-free — the reason it reads keys
from source text is that several templates are not valid YAML, and that
constraint is unchanged.

The exit-status contract in the docstring and the CI step in
.github/workflows/checks.yml both assume "any finding means exit 1". The
docstring MUST be updated to say which lines are advisory and that they do not
affect exit status.
acceptance_criteria:
- [ ] scripts/check-template-drift.py reports each schema-defined optional property a template omits (`known - keys`), alongside the two existing directions
- [ ] Those lines are advisory: a run whose only findings are advisory exits 0
- [ ] A run with any template/missing-required or template/unknown-property finding still exits 1, unchanged
- [ ] The module docstring states which lines are advisory and that they do not affect exit status
- [ ] The script remains dependency-free and performs no YAML parse
- [ ] Run against the current tree, the advisory count is recorded on this bead — the inventory is the point, and it is what a later decision on gating would rest on
- [ ] The CI step in .github/workflows/checks.yml needs no change, because exit status is unchanged for the existing two directions

metadata.tier_reason: one set difference plus a severity decision the Design narrows to two options with a recommendation; localized to a single script

title: Templates become first-class: spec new scaffolding and a placeholder vocabulary
description:
Deferred until there is a payoff other than skipping. Ignore patterns (agent-plugins-qz9.1) cover the immediate need without inventing vocabulary.

The genuine feature is checking templates, not skipping them, and it has a distinct rule shape:
  * instance rules relax - <YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM:SSZ> is legal where a timestamp is required, adr-<nnn> is legal where the slug pattern applies
  * structural rules tighten - the property set must match its type schema exactly, because every document authored from it inherits that set

The structural half is already delivered standalone by scripts/check-template-drift.py, which needs neither the template concept nor the corpus. Build this bead when the driver is scaffolding: `spec new <type>` needs the CLI to know which file is the template for which type, and a declared placeholder vocabulary lets it prompt for each one.

Why templates deserve the attention eventually: they are the most-copied and least-checked artifacts in the framework, and they ship to every adopting repository, so a drifted template distributes a defect at the source.

Do not build a `template: true` flag whose only meaning is skip - it would have to invert its meaning when this bead lands.
acceptance_criteria: The CLI can scaffold a document of a given type from its registered template; placeholders are a declared convention rather than a filename accident.
notes: Deferred by owner 2026-08-12.

title: Decide the defect/issue flow: keep RFCs, or generalise into a defect document type
description:
The framework has one complete flow: greenfield feature -> FRD -> feature blueprint -> work orders. There is no equivalent for defects and issues.

The RFC concept currently absorbs some of that load, and it is unclear whether RFCs survive as-is or generalise into a defect/issue document type. Two distinct things are conflated in the current single `rfc` type: inbound proposals from other repositories using this plugin (correspondence), and this project reporting defects against its own specs (work).

Blocks the corpora-visibility bead, because where rfcs/ documents live and what namespace they belong to depends on this answer.

Related: agent-plugins-j5n - work-order is not in the DocumentType vocabulary at all, so the output artifact of the one flow that does exist is unmodeled.
acceptance_criteria: A decision is recorded on whether RFCs remain, generalise, or split; if a defect flow is adopted, its document types and their place in the corpus are specified.
notes: Deferred by owner 2026-08-12.

title: bb-close-bead.sh header one-liner still says "tracker export"
description:

The export was retired by agent-plugins-92q.31 and `bd dolt push` was added as step 5, so the one-liner is wrong twice — it names a step that no longer runs and omits the one that makes a closure durable.

The same file BODY documents the retirement correctly (the step-2 comment block and the Usage note), so this is a stale summary above accurate detail — the shape most likely to be believed by a reader skimming the header.

- [ ] Line 2 names the real steps: atomic close, verify against the database, stage code, single commit, dolt push

title: Reconsider a task tool as a non-authoritative display mirror of the run checklist
description:
`agent-plugins-ht3` inverted the progress-visibility default: the run checklist
copied into the orchestrator's response is now the default, and a task tool is
the exception for projects with no durable tracker of their own. The reviewer
then asked whether that goes too far, on `pre-flight-check.sh:416`:

> So we might consider adopting `TaskCreate` to produce checklists that provide
> a progress/checklist user experience that is more integrated within the
> agentic app (Claude Desktop, Claude Code, Cursor, etc)?

That is a different question from the one `ht3` answered. `ht3` was about
**tracking** — and there the reasoning holds: a task list duplicates `bd`, dies
with the container, and may not exist in a subagent at all. This is about
**presentation**: a markdown checklist in a transcript is inert text, while a
task tool renders as native UI the user can watch without reading the
conversation.

Those can both be true. The run checklist can stay the durable record while a
task tool mirrors it for display, provided the mirror is explicitly
non-authoritative and nothing ever reads state back from it.

**Evidence this run produced, for both sides.** Waves 1-3 ran with the
checklist only, and the user could follow progress — but the orchestrator also
lost 9.4 hours to an orphaned dispatch that no visible surface reported. A
native progress UI would not have caught that either (the agent believed the
bead was live), so this is a UX improvement, not a correctness one, and should
not be sold as the latter.
design:
Decide, then implement the decision — the analysis is most of the work.

**The question to settle:** does a task tool earn its place as a
*display mirror* of the run checklist, given that `ht3` correctly removed it as
a *tracking* mechanism?

Constraints any answer must respect:

- **`bd` stays the only tracker.** Nothing reads state back from the task tool;
  it is write-only, derived from the checklist. Two dependency graphs is the
  hazard `ht3` removed and this must not reintroduce it.
- **Subagents may have no task tool.** Verified: a subagent in this cloud
  session has no `TaskCreate`, `TaskUpdate` or `TodoWrite`. So only the
  orchestrator could mirror, and the skill must degrade silently where the tool
  is absent rather than treating it as an error.
- **The project ban is real and wins.** This repo's `CLAUDE.md` says "do NOT use
  TodoWrite, TaskCreate". WHERE a project bans it, the mirror does not happen —
  `pre-flight-check.sh` already emits `BB_TASKCREATE`. Any adoption must be
  opt-in per project, not a default that this project then has to suppress.
- **It is presentation, not correctness.** Do not let it accrete
  responsibilities; the moment recovery reads it, it has become a tracker.

**WHEN the answer is yes:** state in `SKILL.md` that the checklist is the record
and the task tool is an optional non-authoritative mirror, gated on the
pre-flight signal, orchestrator-only. One paragraph, not a phase.

**WHEN the answer is no:** record the rejection and the reasoning in `ht3`'s
history so it is not relitigated, and close this as rejected. A recorded no is a
result.

Ask the user which they want before implementing — the trade is a UX preference,
not a technical fact, and it is theirs.
acceptance_criteria:
- [ ] The decision is recorded either way, with reasoning, in a place a future reader will find
- [ ] IF adopted: SKILL.md states the checklist is authoritative and the task tool is an optional orchestrator-only mirror gated on BB_TASKCREATE
- [ ] IF adopted: nothing anywhere reads state back from the task tool
- [ ] IF rejected: the rejection and its reasoning are recorded in ht3's history so it is not relitigated
- [ ] ht3's inversion is not undone in either case
- [ ] The user was asked before implementation, since the trade is a UX preference
close_reason:
REJECTED by user decision, 2026-08-12, after being walked through the options. A recorded no, which this bead's own design names as a valid result.

The bead was right that it asked a different question from agent-plugins-ht3: ht3 settled TRACKING, this asked about PRESENTATION, and both could have been true. Rejected on two grounds.

First, the 'mirror, never source' boundary erodes on first contact with recovery. The moment an orchestrator resuming a dead run reads the task list to see where things got to, it is a tracker, and nothing fails loudly to mark the transition.

Second, budget — an argument this bead did not carry. The skill body is over the ~5,000-token re-injection cap that currently truncates the close ceremony out of a compacted orchestrator's context (agent-plugins-8ef, still open). Spending that budget on an optional display feature, in a repo whose CLAUDE.md bans task tools outright, is the wrong trade now.

Evidence weighed both ways, per the bead's own record: the checklist-only runs were followable, and the 9.4-hour orphaned dispatch that motivated better visibility would NOT have been caught by a task tool either, because the orchestrator believed the bead was live and would have rendered it live. UX, not correctness — the bead said so itself and that is why it loses to a budget argument.

NOT rejected as a bad idea. The fully-specified safe version survives in this bead's Design (write-only, orchestrator-only, gated on pre-flight BB_TASKCREATE, opt-in per project). Reopen from there if the cap problem is solved and the native UI is still wanted. A one-line pointer is in SKILL.md beside the progress-visibility rule so a future reader meets the decision where relitigation would start.

metadata.tier_reason: Small edit whichever way it goes; the value is in recording a decision, and the decision is the user's.

title: spec check never writes the index, so the warm path is never exercised by the workflow the skill prescribes
description:
`spec check` opens the corpus via corpus.Open but never persists the index it
builds; only `spec index` writes `specs/specs.json`. Measured 2026-08-09:

  rm -f specs/specs.json
  spec check   -> specs/specs.json still absent
  spec index   -> specs/specs.json, 215 KB

`specs/specs.json` is gitignored, so a fresh clone has none. The spec skill
never tells an author to run `spec index` — SKILL.md sends them to `spec check`,
`spec refs`, `spec next-id` and `spec slug-exists`. So in the workflow this
tool actually ships for, every invocation is a cold rebuild and the warm path
never runs.

Nothing is incorrect: warm and cold outputs are byte-identical, verified both
corpus-wide and single-document with --json on an edited corpus. And it costs
nothing today — at 36 documents, process start dominates completely:

  corpus wide, cold   median 35.2 ms | p95 58.3 ms
  corpus wide, warm   median 37.8 ms | p95 40.3 ms
  single doc,  cold   median 33.9 ms | p95 37.6 ms
  single doc,  warm   median 33.3 ms | p95 48.5 ms

But it means AC-SPEC-009.1's warm-index latency budget is claimed against a
path no user reaches, and the content-fingerprint machinery it is built on is
unexercised outside tests — which is how agent-plugins-fe1's unreachable code
survived review in the first place.

Decide one of: have `check` write the index it built (making the budget real,
at the cost of a check that writes a file); tell authors to run `spec index`
first, in the skill; or accept it and stop claiming the warm budget for this
workflow. The measurement above says there is no user-visible urgency — this
is about the spec matching the tool.
acceptance_criteria: A decision is recorded on whether the check workflow produces a warm index, and AC-SPEC-009.1's warm-index budget either describes a reachable path or is restated to match what ships.
close_reason: Closed

comments.author: Claude
comments.text: Fixed. cmd.openCorpus wraps corpus.Open for check, refs, slug-exists and next-id, persisting the index when the open had to build one — which is what makes AC-SPEC-010.5's own example ('run twice in a row reads specs.json the second time') true of a workflow that never invokes spec index. Best-effort: the write error is discarded, since a read-only checkout or a concurrent-writer race makes the answer no less correct, and AC-SPEC-010.4's atomic replace is corpus.Write's. Verified a check under an unwritable spec root still exits 0. Warm and cold output remain byte-identical. Documented in container-spec-cli.md Data and in the skill's spec-cli.md.

title: Remove STRATA_ACCESS_TOKEN plumbing once strata-lang/strata is public
description:
The strata CLI is provisioned by cloning strata-lang/strata, which is private today. A cloud session with no attached strata checkout therefore needs a fine-grained PAT in STRATA_ACCESS_TOKEN, and that requirement has plumbing in three places:

- .claude/hooks/session-start.sh — the credential helper (STRATA_CRED_HELPER), the -c credential.helper flags on both clone attempts, the reassertion on the owned clone, and the unset-token warning.
- docs/session-bootstrap.md — the token paragraph and the helper in the pasted setup script.
- AGENTS.md / CLAUDE.md — one sentence each pointing at the requirement.

When the repository goes public the clone succeeds unauthenticated and all of
it becomes dead weight. Delete it rather than leaving it as a no-op: it is the
single largest source of environment-specific prose in the agent instructions,
and it explains a constraint that no longer exists.

Local sessions are unaffected either way — strata is already on PATH there.
acceptance_criteria: No reference to STRATA_ACCESS_TOKEN remains in the hook, the docs, or the agent instruction files; a cloud session with no attached strata checkout still gets a working strata binary.

title: Evaluate pinning index schema_version with == instead of a regex pattern
description:
`schemas/index.strata:345` declares the index schema version as a pattern:

```strata
schema_version: String ~= /^1\.0$/
```

Strata also supports pinning a scalar to a single value with `==`
(`String`, `Bool`, integer types), which makes the property a constant —
documented at `.claude/skills/strata/references/language-reference.md:450-476`:
"Pin a `String`, `Bool`, or integer type to a single value with `==`. The
property becomes a constant."

The two are equivalent for validation here (`^1\.0$` admits exactly `1.0`),
but they differ in what is generated. A pattern yields a validated `String`
field; `==` yields a constant. Because the schema uses the pattern form, the
emitted value has to live somewhere else — `cli/core/specindex.SchemaVersion`,
a package that exists partly because `scripts/generate-schemas.sh` rebuilds
`cli/core/specmodel/` from scratch on every run and so cannot hold
hand-written constants.

Raised by the strata author in review of PR #16: "Strata does support `==`
constraints for scalars (strings, integers, booleans) which are effectively
constant values. It might not be what you needed but FYI."

Note the skill already documented this — `language-reference.md:451` has
carried it all along. The gap was not missing information; the architecture
blueprint simply asserted "Strata has no notion of a constant", which was
false. That claim is corrected in this PR; this bead is the substantive
follow-up.
design:
Evaluate, do not assume it is an improvement.

**In favour.** `schema_version: String == "1.0"` states the intent directly
(this IS the version, not a value matching a shape), and if the Go emitter
renders it as a constant it removes `cli/core/specindex.SchemaVersion` and the
test that guards the pattern/value agreement
(`cli/core/specindex/specindex_test.go:29,91`) — one fewer place for the two
to drift.

**Against, and what to check first.**

1. **What does the Go emitter actually generate for `==`?** Build a scratch
   `.strata` with `foo: String == "1.0"`, run `strata build --target rust` and
   `--target go`, and read the output. If it emits a plain field plus a
   validation rule rather than a constant, this buys nothing and the bead
   closes as declined.
2. **Does it change the JSON Schema?** `==` most likely emits `const` where the
   pattern emits `pattern`. Confirm against
   `cli/core/schema/*.schema.json` and check nothing consuming those schemas
   depends on `pattern`.
3. **Does it change decode behaviour for a wrong version?** Today an index
   carrying `schema_version: "2.0"` fails the pattern. Confirm `==` rejects it
   the same way and with a comparable message — the CLI relies on that
   rejection to refuse an index it cannot read.
4. **Regeneration cost.** Any change to `schemas/index.strata` requires
   `scripts/generate-schemas.sh` and re-committing every generated artifact.
   Cheap, but it must land in one change.

**If adopted**, update `specs/architecture/module-document-core.md` in the same
change — it currently explains why the constant lives in a separate package,
and that explanation stops being true.

**If declined**, record the reason in the blueprint so the next reader does not
re-raise it.

title: SKILL.md: invert the TaskCreate default so the run checklist is the default and a task list is the exception
description:
Two small correctness defects in `bead-bonanza/SKILL.md`, both found comparing
the skill against the current Claude Code documentation and this container's
actual environment.

**1. The `TaskCreate` default is inverted (`SKILL.md:124`).** It reads: "This
skill defaults to `TaskCreate`/`TaskUpdate` for orchestrator-side progress
visibility. If the project's `CLAUDE.md`/`AGENTS.md` explicitly bans
`TaskCreate` ... skip it."

Defaulting to that tool is wrong on three counts: it duplicates the durable
tracker the whole skill is built around (`bd`), its list is session-scoped and
dies with the container, and **it may not exist at all** — a subagent in this
cloud session has no `TaskCreate`, `TaskUpdate` or `TodoWrite` tool. The role
it could uniquely play (in-conversation visibility distinct from durable
tracking) is already filled by the Run checklist the skill copies into its
response at `SKILL.md:34-52`, which is strictly better here: it survives in the
transcript, a human can read it, and it creates no second dependency graph.

**2. Phase 0 does not check `CLAUDE_CODE_SUBAGENT_MODEL`.** Subagent model
resolution order is `CLAUDE_CODE_SUBAGENT_MODEL` env var → per-invocation
`model` → frontmatter → main conversation. The env var **overrides** the
per-invocation parameter. If it is set in a cloud environment, every tier
assignment in the dispatch plan is silently ignored and the Phase 4 escalation
table — which the skill calls "the run's only direct evidence about whether
grooming's routing is calibrated" (`SKILL.md:485-487`) — becomes fiction.

It is NOT set in this container (verified), so this is a latent trap rather
than an observed failure.
design:
**1. Invert the TaskCreate rule.** Make the Run checklist the default and the
task list the exception:

> **Progress visibility.** The Run checklist copied into your response is the
> default and is sufficient. Some projects additionally offer `TaskCreate`/
> `TaskUpdate`; use them only where the project has no durable tracker of its
> own, and never alongside one — two dependency graphs is a correctness hazard,
> not redundancy. Note that a subagent in a cloud session may have no task tool
> at all.

**2. Add the env-var check to Phase 0**, alongside the existing no-delegation
fallback check:

> **Check `CLAUDE_CODE_SUBAGENT_MODEL`.** If it is set, it overrides the
> per-invocation `model` on every dispatch, so tier routing does not happen and
> the Phase 4 escalation table means nothing. Say so once in the dispatch plan
> and omit the escalation table from the final report rather than printing a
> table that cannot be true.

Both edits are small and touch only `SKILL.md`. They should ride along with the
restructure bead rather than being a separate pass over the same file — hold
this until that one is in flight, or fold it in.

Two further native affordances were identified as worth adopting but are NOT
part of this bead; file separately if wanted:
- `SendMessage` to a still-live subagent for skip reconciliation and mid-flight
  correction, instead of the current re-dispatch path.
- `skills: [groom-beads]` frontmatter on the grooming subagent, which injects
  the full skill body rather than relying on the subagent to invoke it.
acceptance_criteria:
- [ ] SKILL.md makes the copied-in run checklist the default progress-visibility mechanism
- [ ] TaskCreate/TaskUpdate are described as an exception for projects with no durable tracker, never alongside one
- [ ] The text notes that a subagent in a cloud session may have no task tool at all
- [ ] Every downstream reference to the Phase 0 TaskCreate step (Phase 1, Phase 3 step 2, Operating principles) is updated to match
- [ ] SKILL.md states the consequence of CLAUDE_CODE_SUBAGENT_MODEL being set: no tier routing, and the escalation table is omitted rather than printed
- [ ] The bd-based task tracking the project mandates is untouched
notes:
## Scope narrowed 2026-08-10

The second half of this bead — checking `CLAUDE_CODE_SUBAGENT_MODEL` in Phase 0 —
has moved into the pre-flight script bead, which is where every other Phase 0
environment probe now lives. The consequence this bead documented still stands
and belongs in SKILL.md: WHEN that variable is set it overrides the
per-invocation `model` on every dispatch, so tier routing does not happen and
the Phase 4 escalation table means nothing; the plan says so once and the report
omits the table rather than printing one that cannot be true. Keep that
sentence here; the detection is the script's.

This bead therefore covers the TaskCreate inversion only.

metadata.tier_reason: One rule inverted plus a mechanical sweep of its downstream references; the second half moved to the pre-flight bead.

comments.author: Claude
comments.text:
retro: DECISION (user, 2026-08-12) — your inversion STANDS, and the reviewer's
follow-up is rejected. Recorded here so it is not relitigated from this bead's
side.

You made the run checklist the default progress surface and demoted the task
tool to an exception for projects with no durable tracker. The PR #18 reviewer
then asked whether that went too far, proposing a task tool as a
progress/checklist UX "more integrated within the agentic app". That was filed

Rejected anyway, on two grounds:

   first time a recovering orchestrator glances at the task list to see where a
   dead run got to. Nothing fails loudly at that moment; it has simply become a
   second tracker, which is the hazard you removed.
2. Budget. The skill body is over the ~5,000-token re-injection cap, which
   currently truncates the close ceremony out of a compacted orchestrator's
   context. Spending any of that on an optional display feature — in a repo
   whose CLAUDE.md bans task tools outright — is the wrong trade while
   agent-plugins-8ef is still open.

Explicitly NOT rejected as a bad idea. If the cap problem is solved and someone
wants the native progress UI, 92q.32 carries a fully-specified safe version:
write-only, orchestrator-only, gated on the pre-flight BB_TASKCREATE signal,
opt-in per project. Reopen from there rather than re-deriving it.

title: contract-specs-configuration.md's internal surface claims required-sections/block-tag registration that corpus.Profile does not deliver
description:
[[contract-specs-configuration]]'s "internal surface: profile registration"
section states that a profile supplies "the section hierarchy it
requires, and the named section sets a span query can select. It
additionally supplies the fenced block tags to extract and any rule that
cannot be expressed as data — the record-XOR-blueprint-link invariant and
supersession integrity are the two current examples," and illustrates it
with a `Section` struct.

The actual `corpus.Profile` interface (cli/core/corpus/profile.go, as
widened by 9kb.2/XPT) has exactly four methods: Schema, DocumentTypes,
Conventions, Lifecycle. `DocumentTypeRules` carries SlugPattern, Numbered,
ReferenceProperties, TypedReferenceProperties, and Pairings — no
required-sections tree, no block-tag registration, no custom-invariant
hook. profile.go's own package comment confirms this is intentional:
"Element records and required sections are later capabilities, and each
will widen this interface further." A repo-wide search
(`RequiredSection`, `BlockTagRegistration`, `type Section struct`) finds
those identifiers only in cli/core/specmodel/specmodel.go (the generated
spec-index data model) and nowhere in a live Go interface consumed by the
CLI.

So the contract currently describes a surface larger than what
`corpus.Profile` actually delivers today. This predates the
reference-integrity feature and is out of scope for agent-plugins-9kb.9,
whose Design section only asked for the four additive enumerations
(reference-bearing properties, typed references, pairings, lifecycle).
Revise the Required Sections / block-tag / invariant paragraph to
describe current behaviour accurately — either as a stated future
capability (matching profile.go's own "later capabilities" framing) or
by removing the claim if no such registration path exists at all, per
c4-guide.md's rule that a contract misdescribing its own surface is
worse than one that is silent.

title: RFC-0012 P6: mark depends_on aspirational
description:
Adopted at triage of rfcs/inbox/spec/rfc-0012-document-relationship-vocabulary.md (P6) on 2026-08-06. Option (b) taken, per the RFC's own recommendation.

## Problem
SystemBlueprint.depends_on appears on 0 corpus documents, so it reads as a
maintained relationship the corpus does not track. But it is the one
relationship with no other home: a system->system dependency is neither
composition nor a contract, and a top-level system has no parent to own it

## Change
schemas/frontmatter.strata: annotate the depends_on doc-comment as
aspirational — recorded on the system's own Context view, unused in the
corpus so far, and explicitly NOT paired (the 'depended-on-by' direction is
derived from the index's inbound edges). Then run generate-schemas.sh.

Do not drop the property; do not add a pairing.

## Acceptance
- generate-schemas.sh --check clean

title: Confirm the POSIX-semantics rename support matrix on Windows
description:
cli/core/corpus/sharing_windows.go falls back to SetFileInformationByHandle with FileRenameInfoEx and FILE_RENAME_POSIX_SEMANTICS when MoveFileEx refuses to replace a file readers hold open. Two support questions behind that are unresolved, and neither is answered by Microsoft's own documentation — the Flags field description on the FILE_RENAME_INFO page is empty, as is the FileRenameInfoEx entry in FILE_INFO_BY_HANDLE_CLASS.

1. Minimum Windows version. The Windows 10 1607 SDK headers (10.0.14393.0) already gate both FILE_RENAME_FLAG_POSIX_SEMANTICS and FileRenameInfoEx on _WIN32_WINNT_WIN10_RS1, which points at 1607/Server 2016. Secondary sources say 1709. Cygwin behaves as if 1809 (has_posix_rename_semantics first appears in wincap_10_1809) though that is confounded by it also passing FILE_RENAME_IGNORE_READONLY_ATTRIBUTE, which genuinely is 1809.

2. Filesystem. Every implementation surveyed (Cygwin, git, Rust) restricts POSIX rename to local NTFS and excludes remote/SMB. No authoritative statement was found about ReFS in either direction.

The code does not depend on an answer: an unsupported filesystem or OS reports ERROR_INVALID_PARAMETER, the fallback returns the original MoveFileEx error, and behaviour is exactly what it was before the fallback existed. So this is a documentation and confidence task, not a defect.

Work: establish the real floor for both, from Microsoft sources if they can be reached (learn.microsoft.com and devblogs.microsoft.com are both blocked by this environment's egress proxy — the SDK header evidence above came from a header mirror). Then either state the supported matrix in a comment in sharing_windows.go, or add runtime feature detection if the floor turns out to be above a version the project intends to support. Windows CI covers only windows-latest, so a version floor below that is untested by construction — note that either way.

title: ContainerBlueprint declares no version property while ModuleBlueprint does
description:
Discovered during agent-plugins-bge.15, which could not satisfy its own
acceptance criterion "version bumped on each" for the container blueprint.

`ModuleBlueprint` declares a `version` property; `ContainerBlueprint` does not,
and the generated schema sets `additionalProperties: false`. So adding
`version:` to `specs/architecture/container-spec-cli.md` fails the corpus
check. bge.15 bumped the two module blueprints 0.1 -> 0.2 and updated the
container's `updated_at` only, and reported the gap rather than forcing it.

Verified against the generated schema:
    ContainerBlueprint  version property: False
    ModuleBlueprint     version property: True

This is an authoring decision, not a defect to patch blindly. Either
containers legitimately carry no version (and every instruction telling an
agent to bump one is wrong for containers), or the asymmetry is an oversight
in `schemas/frontmatter.strata` and ContainerBlueprint should gain the
property like modules have. SystemBlueprint and ComponentBlueprint should be
checked at the same time — the answer probably applies to all C4 levels
uniformly.

Blocks nothing in the current feature. Same class as agent-plugins-tff: a
workflow instruction that the project's own schema cannot express.

title: Tracker Reconciliation's agent-plugins-6n4 note assumes a broader corpus root than the resolved specs/ self-application gate
description:
# agent-plugins-mvx — Tracker Reconciliation's agent-plugins-6n4 note assumes a broader corpus root than the resolved specs/ self-application gate

## Description

specs/features/spec-index/spec-index-blueprint.md's Tracker Reconciliation
says of agent-plugins-6n4 (work-order-template.md is not valid YAML):

    out-of-scope (coordination): work-order-template.md is not valid

agent-plugins-bge.14 resolved (comment, 2026-08-04, author confirmation)
that the self-application gate's corpus root is specs/ (27 markdown
documents), not docs/. agent-plugins-6n4's file is
plugin/skills/spec/references/work-order-template.md — outside specs/
entirely. Verified by running corpus.Build against specs/ per bge.14:
the built index and its one exclusion (specs/adrs/README.md,
no-frontmatter) contain no entry or exclusion for anything under
plugin/skills/, and no exclusion or finding correlates with 6n4's file.

So, as scoped, the self-application gate literally cannot report 6n4 —
the blueprint's Tracker Reconciliation sentence was accurate only under
a broader (or pre-reorg) notion of corpus root, and is now stale in the
same way the Definition of Done's docs/ anchor was. bge.14 could not
satisfy its own fourth acceptance criterion ("agent-plugins-6n4 is
confirmed as surfaced by the gate") to the letter for this reason; see
its retro for how that was handled instead.

This is filed for whoever verifies the Definition of Done and retires
the blueprint (agent-plugins-bge.16) to reconcile: either correct the
Tracker Reconciliation sentence to say the self-application gate does
not cover this file (6n4 stays open via some other regression check —

title: Re-tighten the Rfc schema once Strata supports per-variant requirements
description:
RFC 0010 (`rfcs/inbox/feature-blueprint/rfc-0010-corpus-validation-coverage-and-blueprint-reconciliation.md`,
proposal P2) closes a gap where the `Rfc` model cannot represent a
project-audience RFC: it makes `skill`, `skill_version`, `model`,
`effort` and `runs_observed` OPTIONAL on `struct Rfc` so an RFC
critiquing project documents can validate.

That relaxation is a workaround, not the desired model. For
`audience: skill-authors` those five properties are load-bearing —
`retro-skill`'s readiness gate requires every one of them, because a
skill defect is model-relative and triage cannot judge "already fixed?"
without the skill version. Once they are optional, nothing stops a
skill-lens RFC from being filed with all five absent, and the schema
that used to catch that becomes silent.

The correct model is per-variant requirements: `Rfc` discriminated on
`audience`, where the `skill-authors` variant requires the five and the
`project` variant does not.

**Why this is deferred — the blocking Strata limitation.** Strata
structs inherit but a subtype cannot narrow or redeclare an inherited
property, so an `Rfc` variant cannot re-require a property the parent
declared optional. Verified two ways on 2026-08-04:

- `specs/features/spec-index/spec-index-blueprint.md:200` states it as
  approved design: "Strata cannot narrow the inherited `slug` per type"
  — the same limitation, hit in the profile's slug-pattern table, which
  had to move out of the union schema for exactly this reason.
- The Strata language reference (`docs/content/docs/lang.mdx:60-94` in
  `strata-lang/strata`) documents inheritance only as "Common properties
  get defined once and reused", with no override/narrow/redeclare
  facility. The only `@`-overrides are `@tag` and `@discriminator` for
  union members; "Constraints narrow the set of legal values" (line 307)
  applies to a type, not to an inherited property per variant.

**Do not open this until BOTH hold:**
1. RFC 0010 P2 has been adopted and the relaxation has actually shipped
   (otherwise there is no hole to close).
2. Strata supports per-variant narrowing of an inherited property, or an
   equivalent conditional-requirement mechanism.

Check condition 2 against the Strata release notes before starting; if
it is still absent, re-defer rather than working around it a second
time. No change to `strata-lang/strata` is in scope for this repository.
design: Model `Rfc` as a discriminated union on `audience` (project | skill-authors) with per-variant required sets, replacing RFC 0010 P2's blanket-optional relaxation. Regenerate via scripts/generate-schemas.sh. If Strata still cannot narrow inherited properties per variant, the fallback is to keep the properties optional in the schema and enforce the skill-authors requirement in retro-skill's readiness gate — but that is the status quo this bead exists to replace, so prefer re-deferring over adopting the fallback permanently.
acceptance_criteria:
- [ ] `struct Rfc` in `schemas/frontmatter.strata` requires `skill`,
      `skill_version`, `model`, `effort` and `runs_observed` for
      `audience: skill-authors`, and requires none of them for
      `audience: project`.
- [ ] A project-audience RFC with all five absent validates.
- [ ] A skill-authors RFC missing any of the five FAILS validation —
      demonstrated by a case that passes today and fails after the
      change.
- [ ] Generated artifacts are regenerated and
      `scripts/generate-schemas.sh --check` passes.
- [ ] `python3 scripts/validate-corpus.py` passes over the whole corpus,
      including every RFC already in `rfcs/`.
- [ ] The Strata capability relied on is named on this issue (version or
      feature), so the dependency is auditable.

title: Strata regex literals cannot contain a forward slash, even escaped
description: Adjacent, non-blocking. A `~= /.../` regex literal in a .strata source cannot contain `/`: `\/` and `[/]` both fail with a syntax error at the character after the slash (strata 13494ba, observed while writing schemas/finding.strata for agent-plugins-bge.4). Worked around by declaring `alias RuleId: String` with the namespaced kebab-case shape stated in the doc block instead of constrained by a pattern, so rule identifiers like `slug/pattern-mismatch` are unconstrained in the emitted JSON Schema. Upstream fix belongs in strata-lang/strata's lexer; re-add the constraint here when it lands.

title: check-skills.sh does not treat strata-generated markdown as generated
description:
ADJACENT — does not block agent-plugins-bge.1 (worked around).

scripts/check-skills.sh is_generated() recognises a file as generated only when its first line starts with '<!-- GENERATED COPY'. The strata-generated markdown under plugin/skills/spec/references/generated/ carries no such banner, so it is subjected to the backticked-path check: any backticked filename in a .strata doc block (e.g. `specs.json`) becomes 'backticked path does not resolve from this file' — reported twice, once via plugin/skills and once via the .claude/skills symlink — at a location that cannot be hand-edited.

Observed while adding schemas/index.strata; worked around by writing the filename in bold rather than backticks. Fix is either a banner in the generated markdown (scripts/generate-schemas.sh writes a README banner already) or a path skip in check-skills.sh.

title: triage-rfc: should the sequencing escape hatch key on the graph's consumer? (RFC P4)
description:
DEFERRED at triage on 2026-08-01. Not dispatchable as written — the
evidence is self-referential and one more independent observation is
wanted before the rule is changed. Status is 'deferred' so it stays out
of 'bd ready'.

## Problem

`.claude/skills/triage-rfc/SKILL.md:173-175` gives the escape hatch
from the sequencing rule:

    WHERE the approved set is small and touches disjoint files,
    implement inline and say so; grooming a two-file change is
    overhead.

The hatch turns on the SHAPE of the approved set — size and file
disjointness. The variable that has actually decided the question in
practice is different: whether anything will CONSUME the dependency
graph that grooming produces. A single agent implementing inline, with
no dispatch and no parallelism, produces a graph with no reader.

## Evidence (inlined — do not rely on the RFC being at hand)

Two observations, both from model claude-opus-5, both in the session of
2026-08-01, and both made by the agent that authored the rule.

1. The triage that ADOPTED this rule (RFC 0008 P1) then declined to
   follow it. Its approved set was 10 proposals with 6 colliding on one
   file — neither small nor disjoint, so the hatch did not apply and
   the rule required filing 10 beads and running `groom-beads`. The
   agent implemented inline and recorded the deviation in
   `rfcs/rfc-0008-triage-rfc-implementation-sequencing.md` under
   Resolution. Its stated reason was the missing consumer, not the set
   shape. Correctness the rule protects — serialized edits to a shared
   file, version bump last — was obtained by hand and verified.

2. The next triage run hit the same fork: 5 approved changes plus one
   human-reported change, all landing on the same file. The human was
   asked to choose and directed that the rule be followed, which is how
   the beads for that run (including this one) came to exist.

## Why this was deferred rather than adopted

Both observations are the same agent in the same session, so this is
repetition rather than independent corroboration. The RFC proposing it
says so itself: "Triage may reasonably defer it for corroboration from
a run that did not author it."

The cost of deferring is real and should be weighed on any future
recurrence: the rule stays miscalibrated, and the next single-agent
triage either files beads nobody reads or deviates again.

## What would make this ready

Any ONE of:
- A triage run under a different model, or in a different session,
  hitting the same fork and recording what it did.
- A decision that filing the graph is worth it regardless of consumer
  (e.g. because the beads are themselves the audit record) — which
  would close this by rejecting it, not by adopting it.

## The proposed change, if it is ever adopted

Replace SKILL.md:173-175 with:

     WHERE the approved set is small and touches disjoint files, OR
     WHERE the implementation will run in a single agent with no
     dispatch and no parallelism, implement inline and say so —
     sequencing the colliding edits by hand and bumping each file after
     its last change, which is what the graph would have enforced. File
     the graph when something will consume it: parallel agents, a
     `bead-bonanza` run, or work resuming in a later session. A graph
     with no reader is filing, not sequencing.

title: triage-rfc: state that retro-note ingestion is outside the step-4 gate, and bump 1.3->1.4 (RFC P5)
description:
## Problem

`triage-rfc` tells the agent to ingest retro notes — appending to the
retro log and deleting the note file — before step 1, which places two
file mutations above the skill's hard stop at step 4. No text states
that this is a deliberate exemption.

`.claude/skills/triage-rfc/SKILL.md:63-64`:

    Retro notes first: append each to the retro log (step 6), then
    delete the note.

`SKILL.md:60`: "Step 4 is a hard stop. Do not tick 5 before the human
has answered."

## Evidence (inlined — do not rely on the RFC being at hand)

Observed in the triage run of 2026-08-01, model claude-opus-5.

The run ingested `rfcs/inbox/frd/retro-note-frd-authoring-2026-07-31.md`.
Before doing so the agent paused to decide whether writing the log and
deleting an input before the human gate was legitimate, concluded that
a retro note is a null result carrying no proposals so there is nothing
to approve, and wrote that justification into its own response to the
human before proceeding. The conclusion was correct; the skill did not
supply it.

Source: rfcs/inbox/triage-rfc/rfc-self-triage-rfc-evidence-completeness.md,
proposal P5 (severity polish, origin self, runs_observed 1).

## THIS BEAD ALSO OWNS THE VERSION BUMP

This is the LAST bead in the chain of five that change
`.claude/skills/triage-rfc/SKILL.md` in this triage. Per the skill's
own rule (SKILL.md:182-190, "Bump each file exactly once for the whole
triage, no matter how many proposals changed it — ... the bump belongs
to whichever lands last"), this bead performs the single frontmatter
version bump for all five changes. Verify the other four landed first.
design:
Two edits.

1. Replace the retro-notes sentence at SKILL.md:63-64 with:

Retro notes first: append each to the retro log (step 6), then delete
the note. This is deliberately outside the step-4 gate — a retro note
is a null result and carries no proposals, so there is nothing for a
human to approve, and the log stays complete either way. Name each
ingested note in the report.

(No leading indentation; this is body prose, not a numbered step.)

2. Bump the skill frontmatter `version: "1.3"` to `version: "1.4"`.
   MINOR, because all five changes in this chain are normative.

Before making edit 2, confirm the other four beads in this chain have
landed: step 3 carries the Extent/Sufficiency checks and the reworded
already-implemented bullet, step 4 carries the T1..Tn paragraph, and
the step-5 version bullet carries the no-version-property rule.

Do NOT bump `plugin/.claude-plugin/plugin.json`. `triage-rfc` is
repo-local: it has no source directory under `plugin/skills/` and is
tracked only at `.claude/skills/triage-rfc/SKILL.md`, so installs never
receive it. This is the rule at SKILL.md step 7 applied to this skill
itself.
acceptance_criteria:
- [ ] The retro-notes instruction states that ingestion is outside the step-4 gate and why
- [ ] It asks the report to name each ingested note

- [ ] plugin/.claude-plugin/plugin.json is unchanged by this triage
- [ ] The four sibling beads' changes are all present in the file before the bump was made
- [ ] Every line added is at most 80 characters

title: bd auto-export does not propagate deletions to issues.jsonl
description:
Measured 2026-07-31 in this repo, bd 1.1.2, with `export.auto: true` and `interval: 60s` in .beads/config.yaml.

Creating an issue refreshed .beads/issues.jsonl immediately (10 lines to 19). `bd delete` on that same issue did NOT: the deleted record was still in the file after 90 seconds, well past the interval. Only an explicit `bd export > .beads/issues.jsonl` produced a correct file (18 lines, probe absent).

Consequence in this project: because the SessionStart hook rebuilds the database by importing that file, a deleted issue silently comes back in the next session.

Worked around by documenting the explicit export in the session-close steps in CLAUDE.md and AGENTS.md. Worth reporting upstream, and worth re-testing on a bd upgrade — if auto export becomes authoritative the manual step can go.
acceptance_criteria: Either upstream fixes it and the manual export step is removed from CLAUDE.md, or the limitation is confirmed as intended and the workaround stays with a link to the upstream decision
notes: Follow-up test 2026-07-31: the beads PRE-COMMIT hook uses the same append/update path, so it does not rescue a deletion either. Sequence: create probe -> commit (file gains it, 21 lines) -> bd delete probe -> commit again (file STILL has it, 21 lines). An earlier commit that printed 'Exported 20 issues' and produced a correct file was correct only because an explicit bd export had been run moments before. Conclusion: an explicit 'bd export > .beads/issues.jsonl' is the only form that reflects deletions.
close_reason: Premise dead, verified 2026-08-12. All three rest on .beads/*.jsonl being tracked in git and being the carrier of issues between sessions. It is not: 'git ls-files .beads/' lists only .gitignore, README.md, config.yaml, metadata.json and the hooks — no JSONL — and .beads/.gitignore:87-89 ignores issues.jsonl, issues-full.jsonl and interactions.jsonl. The Dolt remote (refs/dolt/data) is the source of truth and the SessionStart hook does no JSONL import. Two branches cannot conflict on a file git does not track; a deleted issue cannot return via an import that does not happen; and a stale issues-full.jsonl is not tracked so cannot be 'stale in git'.

title: .beads/issues-full.jsonl is stale and malformed
description:
The file is tracked in git but nothing regenerates it. It holds 4 issues against .beads/issues.jsonl's 10, and its final line parses to a record with a null id.

The risk is that it looks authoritative. .beads/issues.jsonl is the durable export the SessionStart hook restores from (.claude/hooks/session-start.sh); issues-full.jsonl participates in nothing.

Either delete it, or establish what regenerates it and when.

title: frontmatter: can 'sources' record an input that is not a spec document? (RFC 0006 P4)
description:
DEFERRED at triage on 2026-07-31. Not dispatchable as written — the scope decision below is unmade. Status is 'deferred' so it stays out of 'bd ready'.

## Problem

A 'sources' frontmatter property is defined as holding SLUGS ONLY:
'plugin/skills/spec/references/frontmatter-standards.md:119' declares
'sources: []   # Source document slugs'. The FRD template repeats it at
'plugin/skills/spec/references/frd-template.md:8' — 'slugs of documents
this FRD is based on'.

But documents outside the specification set have no slug BY DESIGN.
'plugin/skills/spec/references/cross-document-references.md:124-125'
states: 'The [[document-slug]] notation SHALL be reserved for documents
in the specification set; it SHALL NOT be used for documents outside
it.' Research briefs, vendor docs and prior-art reviews are correctly
out-of-set and correctly slugless.

So an FRD derived from an out-of-set input cannot record that fact.

## Evidence (inlined — do not rely on the RFC being at hand)

'docs/frds/FRD-spec-validation-cli.md' was derived almost entirely from
'docs/plans/spec-validation-cli-brief.md', a ~700-line research brief
carrying prototype measurements and nine resolved scope questions. The
brief is correctly not a spec document and correctly has no slug. The
FRD therefore ships with 'sources: []' — which is FALSE. Its only record
of provenance is one backticked path in the References prose section.

The index specified by that same FRD (REQ-SPEC-002) would report the
document as having no sources at all.

## Why this was deferred rather than adopted

The RFC proposed changing 'frd-template.md:8' alone. Triage rejected
that scope: 'frontmatter-standards.md' OWNS the property, so changing
one template alone would make a template contradict its standard — which
is precisely the defect class P1 of the same RFC was adopted to remove
(the ADR template contradicting the prefix registry, which produced 11
non-conforming slugs and 26 dangling references).

Three templates carry a 'sources' property:
  plugin/skills/spec/references/frd-template.md
  plugin/skills/spec/references/feature-blueprint-template.md
  plugin/skills/spec/references/work-order-template.md

## What must be decided before this is groomable

1. Should 'sources' accept a mixed list (slugs for in-set documents,
   repo-relative paths for out-of-set ones), or should a SECOND property
   carry out-of-set inputs? A mixed list keeps one property but makes
   every consumer discriminate two value shapes; a second property keeps
   each shape clean but adds vocabulary to a deliberately small set.
2. Whichever is chosen, 'frontmatter-standards.md' changes FIRST as the
   owner, then the three templates follow in the same change.
3. Does the same treatment apply to 'related', which has the identical
   slugs-only constraint?

Source: rfcs/rfc-0006-spec-reference-bundles-and-adr-slug.md, proposal
P4. Retro that produced it: rfcs/retro-note-frd-authoring-2026-07-31.md
design:
NOT AN IMPLEMENTATION PLAN — the three questions above are unmade decisions. A grooming pass can only start once a human picks (1) and confirms (3).

Whichever shape wins, the change ORDER is fixed: frontmatter-standards.md (the owner) first, then frd-template.md, feature-blueprint-template.md and work-order-template.md in the same commit, each with its instruction-block Version bumped, plus the plugin version. Landing a template ahead of the standard reproduces the exact contradiction P1 was adopted to remove.
acceptance_criteria:
- [ ] A human has chosen mixed-list vs second-property, and answered whether 'related' gets the same treatment.
- [ ] frontmatter-standards.md defines the chosen form, and its version is bumped.
- [ ] All three templates carrying 'sources' match that definition, each with its instruction-block Version bumped.
- [ ] No template states a rule about 'sources' that frontmatter-standards.md does not.

title: templates: placeholder section lists convey nothing (RFC P4)
description:
GROOMING OUTCOME: blocked-ungroomable. NOT dispatchable. Do not hand
this bead to an implementing agent — the change it describes is defective
as written and its scope is undecided. See "Why this is blocked" below
and the reshape requirements in Design. Status is `deferred` so it stays
out of `bd ready`.

Source: `rfcs/inbox/rfc-self-spec-document-self-check.md`, proposal P4
(severity polish, origin self, runs_observed 1, model claude-opus-5).
Filed by an RFC triage pass that stopped at step 4 on human instruction;
nothing was implemented. The triage recommendation was DEFER.

PROBLEM AS REPORTED
`plugin/skills/spec/references/standards-template.md:15-18` reads:

    Sections (complete each, then delete its instruction block)
      - <Major Category>
      - <Another Major Category>
      - References

For a template whose sections are author-defined, this enumerates
placeholders and conveys little. It contrasts with the fixed-section
templates — ADR (Context / Decision / Alternatives Considered /
Consequences / References) — where the same list is a genuine map.
The RFC proposes replacing the placeholder list with a structural note:
"Structure: one `##` per major requirement category, `###` per
subcategory, then a References section. Categories are author-defined;
name them for the domain, not for this template."

WHY THIS IS BLOCKED (three findings, all verified during grooming)

1. The proposed change breaks the repo's own gate.
   `scripts/check-skills.sh:132-136` fails any file under
   `plugin/skills/*/references/` longer than 100 lines that has no line
   matching `^#+ Contents` or `^Sections \(complete`:

       for p in glob.glob('plugin/skills/*/references/*.md'):
           if '/shared/' in p: continue
           t = open(p).read()
           if len(t.split('\n')) > 100 and not re.search(
                   r'^#+ Contents|^Sections \(complete', t, re.M):
               err(p, "over 100 lines with no table of contents")

   `standards-template.md` is 218 lines and clears that gate only via
   its line 15, "Sections (complete each, then delete its instruction
   block)" — the exact line P4 deletes. The RFC's replacement text
   matches neither alternation branch, so applying P4 verbatim makes
   `scripts/check-skills.sh` fail on the very file it edits.

2. The real scope is ten files, and the RFC specifies one.
   Ten templates under `plugin/skills/spec/references/` carry the same
   "Sections (complete each" construct — verified by grep: adr,
   component-blueprint, container-blueprint, contract, feature-blueprint,
   frd, module-blueprint, standards, system-blueprint, work-order. The
   RFC addresses only the author-defined-section case and does not say
   which of the ten keep their enumerated list. A dispatched agent would
   have to invent that taxonomy decision.

3. No run cost, so nothing forces the call now. The RFC's own
   justification is "worth doing while the section lists are being
   reviewed for other reasons" — it records no evidence that the
   placeholder list harmed a run.
design:
NOT AN IMPLEMENTATION PLAN. This bead is blocked-ungroomable; what
follows is what a human must decide before it can be re-groomed, and
what a reshaped change would have to satisfy.

UNBLOCK CRITERIA (any implementing work needs all three settled)

A. A human adopt/defer decision. The current recommendation is DEFER,
   pending a second, independent project reporting the same friction —
   at which point the `theme:template-ergonomics` label makes the
   recurrence countable.

B. A scope decision naming, of the ten templates carrying the
   "Sections (complete each" construct (adr, component-blueprint,
   container-blueprint, contract, feature-blueprint, frd,
   module-blueprint, standards, system-blueprint, work-order), which
   are in scope for the structural note and which keep their enumerated
   list. The RFC treats this as a one-file edit; it is not.

C. A gate strategy, picking exactly one of:
   - keep a line matching `^Sections \(complete` in every touched file
     over 100 lines; or
   - add a `## Contents` heading to every touched file over 100 lines;
     or
   - deliberately amend the regex at `scripts/check-skills.sh:135` to
     accept the new form, as its own reviewed change.

A reshaped bead would also have to bump each touched template's
instruction-block `Version`, plus
`plugin/.claude-plugin/plugin.json`.

WHY NOT blocked-needs-info: the block is not one missing fact. Even
given a human "adopt", the change still needs redesign (B and C), so
this is a redesign block, not an information block.

title: Decide whether retired documents are exempt from reference checks
description:
Deferred: zero instances in this repository today.

The principle, if adopted: a check that asks a document to change should not fire on a document that will never change again. A retired document is closed, and its references are frozen.

Two cases must not be conflated:
  (a) a live document citing a retired one - reference/retired-target. Valuable, keep on. All 10 occurrences in rfcs/ are this case, from documents with status: ready-for-review, and the check is working correctly.
  (b) a retired document citing anything, live or dead. This is the case for exemption, and it currently has no instances - under a unified root, rfcs/retired/ is entirely clean.

If built: it belongs in specs.toml as repository policy rather than as a CLI flag, because it is a property of the repository and not of the invocation. The existing `unverified` severity fits better than warning - "this reference cannot be confirmed, and nobody is going to" is precisely that state.
acceptance_criteria: Either a policy setting exempts retired documents from reference checks, or the decision to keep checking them is recorded with its rationale.
notes: Deferred by owner 2026-08-12.

title: Several corpora with declared one-way visibility, rather than one corpus with many roots
description:
Deferred: blocked on deciding what rfcs/ becomes.

specs/ and the skills references/ must not resolve against each other - the specs describe how the plugin was built, the references ship inside the plugin, and bundling them would ship consumers a pointer to documents they do not have. A multi-root corpus would quietly create exactly that coupling, so it is the wrong feature.

The right shape is several corpora, each its own slug namespace, with declared one-way visibility: rfcs may cite specs; specs cite nothing outside themselves; the skills references cite nothing at all. That turns a packaging rule into a check - a skill reference citing [[adr-012]] should fail, and today nothing catches it.

Blocked on: whether the RFC concept survives, or generalises into a defect/issue document type feeding a defects -> work orders flow. Observation worth holding: rfcs/ is inbox + outbox + retired, which is a mail queue rather than a corpus. Inbound proposals from other repositories are correspondence about this system, not specifications of it. If that framing holds, document-local checks are the permanent answer for rfcs/ and this bead reduces in scope.

Measured, so the migration cost is known: under one unified root, rfcs/ produces zero unresolved references. The 30+ seen when rooted at rfcs/ alone were root-boundary artifacts, not rot. Real backlog after excluding fixtures and templates is 1 slug pattern mismatch, 3 placeholder citations in c4-guide.md (fixable with backticks, the extractor already skips code spans), and 10 retired-target warnings from live RFCs.
acceptance_criteria: Corpora and their permitted citation directions are declarable; a citation crossing an undeclared boundary is a finding.
notes:
SCOPE CHALLENGED AND ACCEPTED 2026-08-12 (owner): this does not come up unless a repository has multiple spec roots, and that is not demonstrated outside this one.

The challenge holds. An adopting repository has one specs/ directory; the plugin it installs lives outside that root (in the Claude plugins directory), so its shipped documents are never a second corpus there. The need here is an artifact of this being the plugin s OWN development repository — the only place where the documents describing how the plugin was built and the documents the plugin ships both exist in one tree. That is unusual and may stay unique.

What survives the challenge, and what does not:
  * The one-way visibility CHECK (a skill reference citing [[adr-012]] should fail) is a real packaging invariant, but only this repository can violate it, so it protects one repo rather than the framework.
  * The multi-corpus FEATURE is speculative. A monorepo with several products wanting per-product slug namespaces is plausible but has no reported instance.

Kept rather than closed only because it carries the migration measurement, which is expensive to re-derive: under one unified root, rfcs/ produces ZERO unresolved references — the 30+ seen when rooted at rfcs/ alone were root-boundary artifacts. Real backlog after excluding fixtures and templates is 1 slug pattern mismatch, 3 placeholder citations in c4-guide.md, and 10 retired-target warnings from live RFCs.

Close this outright if the measurement is not worth the open bead; it is cheap to re-file if a second adopter ever needs it.
Scope challenged by owner and accepted: needs multiple spec roots, not demonstrated outside this repo.
